terms.gloss: The young con man; on these pages also 'инспектор пожарной охраны', 'технический директор и главный руководитель концессии', 'главный концессионер'.
terms.why_hard: Name must be fixed once (Ostap, not Ostáp/Ostapp); his mock-official self-titles must be rendered as consistent running epithets, not paraphrased away.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, Bender's partner; the narrator alternates surname, name+patronymic and 'предводитель'.
terms.why_hard: Patronymic must not be dropped or turned into a middle initial; transliteration must be stable (Matveyevich vs Matveevich) across the book.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビャーニノフ

terms.gloss: Short for предводитель дворянства, the elected marshal of a district's nobility; the narrator uses it as Vorobyaninov's standing epithet.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'leader' or 'ringleader' loses the pre-revolutionary rank and the joke of a marshal of the nobility kicking a priest.

proposed.ja: 貴族団長

terms.gloss: Priest of the church of Frol and Lavr, rival treasure-hunter; also 'батюшка', 'святой отец', 'духовная особа'.
terms.why_hard: Three different address forms carry three tones (affectionate, sarcastic, mock-solemn); collapsing them to 'Father' everywhere kills the sarcasm of 'святой отец'.

proposed.en: Father Fyodor Vostrikov (батюшка: Father; святой отец: holy father; духовная особа: the reverend gentleman)
proposed.zh: 费奥多尔神父·沃斯特里科夫（батюшка：神父；святой отец：圣父；духовная особа：这位神职人士）
proposed.ja: フョードル・ヴォストリコフ神父（батюшка：神父さま；святой отец：聖なる父よ；духовная особа：聖職者殿）

terms.gloss: Manager of the old-age home, the 'bashful thief' of chapter 8; 'Альхен' is a diminutive of Alexander.
terms.why_hard: The diminutive must be kept as a nickname, not normalised to Alexander; the chapter epithet 'голубой' means bashful/shy, not 'gay'.

proposed.zh: 阿利欣（亚历山大·雅科夫列维奇）
proposed.ja: アリヘン（アレクサンドル・ヤコヴレヴィチ）

terms.gloss: Alkhen's freeloading relative who steals the chair; an old woman mangles his patronymic to 'Мелентьевич'.
terms.why_hard: The mangled patronymic is a deliberate joke and must be preserved as a different name, not silently corrected.

proposed.zh: 帕沙·埃米利耶维奇 / 帕什卡·梅连季耶维奇
proposed.ja: パーシャ・エミリエヴィチ / パーシカ・メレンチエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Alkhen's wife's brothers, all with the patronymic Yakovlevich, lodged and fed at the home; 'уцелевшие Яковлевичи' is a running gag.
terms.why_hard: The plural patronymic used as a family label needs a fixed device ('the Yakovleviches'); losing it loses the joke about a whole clan on state porridge.

proposed.zh: 雅科夫列维奇们（未成年的伊西多尔·雅科夫列维奇）
proposed.ja: ヤコヴレヴィチ一党（未成年のイシドル・ヤコヴレヴィチ）

terms.gloss: The Stargorod Social Security Department's Old-Age Home No. 2, the 'богадельня' where Ostap poses as fire inspector.
terms.why_hard: The acronym Старсобес (Старгородский отдел социального обеспечения) must be unpacked once and reused; leaving 'Starsobes' opaque or calling it a 'nursing home' misleads.

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社会保障局第二养老院
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド社会保障局第二養老院

terms.gloss: The 'red corner': a room in every Soviet workplace or dormitory for political posters, newspapers and meetings.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'red corner' reads as decor; needs the one-time note that it is the agitprop room, then a fixed term.

proposed.ja: 赤いコーナー（政治学習室）

terms.gloss: A foam fire extinguisher, brand 'Eclair', that 'sings' throughout chapter 8 and finally erupts.
terms.why_hard: The mock-technical compound 'пеногон' must sound like a product label, and the brand name must stay consistent so the running gag lands.

proposed.ja: 泡消火器「エクレール」

terms.gloss: Antonina Nezhdanova, celebrated Bolshoi soprano, one of the first to hold the title People's Artist of the Republic.
terms.why_hard: The title must be rendered as an official Soviet honorific, and the reader needs to know she is a famous coloratura for the top-F joke to work.

proposed.en: People's Artist of the Republic Nezhdanova (the soprano)
proposed.zh: 共和国人民演员涅日丹诺娃（女高音歌唱家）
proposed.ja: 共和国人民芸術家ネジダーノワ（ソプラノ歌手）

terms.gloss: Made of or coloured like toile-du-Nord, a cheap grey-blue cotton; the old women's uniform fabric in chapter 8, here a cook's cap and the extinguisher foam.
terms.why_hard: Transliterating 'tualdenor' is meaningless; the colour must be named the same way each time since the narrator keeps reusing it as a joke.

proposed.ja: 灰色木綿（トワル・デュ・ノール）の

terms.gloss: Ostap addresses the old women as 'maidens/girls'; a recurring deadpan mock-gallantry.
terms.why_hard: Must be the same word each time and read as ironic gallantry, not literal description of age.

proposed.zh: 姑娘们（“可悲啊，姑娘们” / “安静点，姑娘们”）
proposed.ja: お嬢さん方（「悲しいことですな、お嬢さん方」／「落ち着いて、お嬢さん方」）

terms.gloss: ДОПР, дом принудительных работ: a 1920s forced-labour prison (Ukrainian SSR term); 'пошел в монахи — сидит в допре' is a prison joke.
terms.why_hard: Must be a prison, not a 'workhouse' or 'monastery'; the reader needs the monk/prison pun to survive.

proposed.ja: 強制労働所（刑務所）

terms.gloss: Ostap's excuse for not hitting Pasha: 'Zarathustra does not permit it', a mock-Nietzschean scruple.
terms.why_hard: Must keep Nietzsche's Zarathustra recognisable (not Zoroaster the prophet) and keep the deadpan tone.

proposed.ja: ツァラトゥストラが許さん

terms.gloss: Ostap's insult: 'abortion victim', i.e. a botched, unwanted specimen of humanity.
terms.why_hard: Literal rendering reads as an accusation about the victim's mother; needs a fixed comic insult that keeps the abortion image.

proposed.ja: この堕胎のし損ないめ

terms.gloss: Ostap misuses nautical jargon: 'cast off the lines, but don't shove off', i.e. stay put.
terms.why_hard: Rendering as plain 'stay here' loses the sailor-talk register that is Ostap's signature; the internal contradiction is the joke.

proposed.en: cast off, but don't shove off
proposed.ja: 綱は解け、だが船は出すな

terms.gloss: Article 114 of the 1926 RSFSR Criminal Code, which Ostap cites (bribing an official) while pocketing the bribe.
terms.why_hard: Keep the number and the mock-legal formula intact; do not 'correct' the article to a modern code.

proposed.ja: 刑法第百十四条

terms.gloss: A ten-ruble note of the 1922-47 gold-backed currency, a substantial bribe.
terms.why_hard: 'Ten rubles' loses the period flavour, 'chervonets' alone is opaque; fix one hybrid rendering for the whole book.

proposed.ja: 十ルーブル金券（チェルヴォーネツ）

terms.gloss: Ostap's catchphrase 'the session continues', echoing the parliamentary formula after an assassination attempt; it became a Russian proverb.
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed formula every time Ostap says it (it recurs across the novel) and sound like an official minute, not casual speech.

proposed.ja: 会議は続行する！

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town ('Old Town') where the first part is set; also in the compounds Старсобес, Старгико, губплан.
terms.why_hard: Never translate as 'Old Town'; transliterate once and keep the same base in all acronyms.

proposed.ja: スタルゴロド

terms.gloss: Soviet acronym institutions: provincial planning commission, mill-construction trust, a Stargorod cooperative or communal-services body.
terms.why_hard: Acronyms are part of the period colour; the translator must choose one policy (transliterate + gloss vs. expand) and apply it to every acronym in the book.

proposed.en: the Gubplan (provincial planning board) / Melstroi (mill-construction trust) / Stargiko
proposed.zh: 省计划委员会 / 磨坊建设托拉斯 / 斯塔尔戈罗德合作社
proposed.ja: 県計画委員会 / 製粉建設トラスト / スタルゴロド協同組合

terms.gloss: 'Lena Events Street', a Soviet renaming after the 1912 Lena goldfields massacre; paired with 'улица Маркса и Энгельса' and 'Большая Пушкинская'.
terms.why_hard: Not the Lena river as scenery: the street name commemorates a massacre and is a joke about revolutionary renaming; keep all street names in one style.

proposed.ja: レナ事件通り

terms.gloss: A chair by Gambs, the Petersburg court furniture firm; the twelve treasure chairs of the title, walnut with bent legs and English chintz.
terms.why_hard: The maker's name must be stable (Gambs, not Hambs/Gamps) since the whole book hunts 'Gambs chairs'.

proposed.ja: ガンブス製の椅子

terms.gloss: The municipal housing department (жилищный отдел) that Vorobyaninov is sent to trace the chairs.
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed rendering as an office name, not 'housing office' one time and 'residential department' the next.

proposed.ja: 住宅課

terms.gloss: Church of Sts Florus and Laurus, patrons of horses, in the folk name forms Frol and Lavr.
terms.why_hard: Choose once between the Latin saints and the Russian folk forms; the folk forms carry the provincial flavour.

proposed.en: the church of St Frol and St Lavr
proposed.ja: フロルとラヴル教会

terms.gloss: A member of the Soviet militia, i.e. the ordinary police.
terms.why_hard: 'Militiaman' vs 'policeman' must be decided once; 'militia' can wrongly suggest paramilitaries to the target reader.

proposed.ja: 民警

terms.gloss: Wrestling term 'par terre' (ground fighting) applied to two men rolling on rubble; not the theatre stalls.
terms.why_hard: The false-friend 'партер' as 'orchestra seats' would make nonsense; keep the sports-commentary register.

proposed.en: the bout continued on the mat
proposed.ja: 闘いはグラウンドに移った

terms.gloss: 'Only horns and legs were left', from the nursery song about the grey goat; means utterly destroyed (echoed later in Ilf & Petrov's 'Рога и копыта').
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering leaves the reader thinking the chair had horns; needs a fixed idiomatic equivalent that keeps the comic image.

proposed.en: nothing left but the horns and the hooves
proposed.ja: 残ったのは角と脚だけ

terms.gloss: A 1920s foxtrot/shimmy hit whose lyric mentions camels and the Botocudos ('ба-та-ку-ды'); Ostap hums it.
terms.why_hard: Verse must be rendered as singable doggerel, and 'ба-та-ку-ды' identified as the Botocudo tribe, not a nonsense word.

proposed.en: 'Shimmy' (Once it was the camels did it, / once the Bo-to-cu-dos shook it, / now the whole wide world is dancing shimmy…)
proposed.zh: 《西迷舞》（从前是骆驼这么跳，/ 从前博托库多人这么跳，/ 如今全世界都跳西迷舞……）
proposed.ja: 『シミー』（昔はラクダがやっていた、/ 昔はボトクード族が踊っていた、/ 今じゃ世界中がシミーを踊る……）

terms.gloss: A newsboy's cry mangling Izvestia, plus the satirical weekly Smekhach and the illustrated Krasnaya Niva.
terms.why_hard: The mispronunciation must be reproduced, and the titles kept as real recognisable periodicals rather than translated descriptively.

proposed.en: Moscow paper Izvestya! Smekhach! Krasnaya Niva!
proposed.zh: 莫斯科报纸《消息报》、《笑匙》杂志、《红色田野》！
proposed.ja: モスクワの新聞『ズヴェスチヤ』、雑誌『スメハーチ』、『赤い畑』！

conventions: Dialogue: replace the Russian speech dash with target-language quotation marks (en “ ”, zh “ ”, ja 「 」); keep the narrator's interjected stage directions as separate clauses.

Names: always give name + patronymic where the Russian does, transliterated once per person (en: Ippolit Matveyevich; zh: 新华社-style transliteration with ·; ja: katakana with long vowels), and preserve deliberate mangling such as Пашка Мелентьевич.

Register: render pre-revolutionary -с (да-с) as an obsequious tag (en 'yes, sir'; zh '是的，先生'; ja 'ですとも'); mark Ostap's switch from вы to ты toward Pasha by blunter address in en/zh and by dropping honorifics (お前, plain form) in ja.

\u0442\u0443\u0434\u044b \u0435\u0435 \u.ja: ブランコにでも突っ込んじまえ

reasons.\u0438\u0437\u0432\u043e\u0437\u0447\u04: The word names the man, not the vehicle, and the horse must stay visible; 'cabby' alone hides it.
reasons.\u00ab\u0411\u044b\u0441\u0442\u0440\u04: Transliteration keeps the Soviet-portmanteau sound, the bracketed gloss delivers the joke once; the third candidate's zh drops the transliteration.
reasons.\u0415\u043b\u0435\u043d\u0430 \u0421\u0: Slash form signals two alternating references (name or 'the fortune-teller') as the Russian does, not a permanent appositive.
reasons.\u043a\u043e\u043d\u0446\u0435\u0441\u04: Aligned with the fuller 'концессионеры / концессия' entry so the running gag has one rendering; 利権事業者 keeps the legal-commercial sense better than 利権屋.
reasons.\u0414\u044b\u0448\u0438\u0442\u0435 \u0: 'Excited' is the natural English of взволнованы and the form readers know from the standard translation; 'agitated' sounds clinical.
reasons.\u0413\u0443\u0441\u0438\u0449\u0435: Bare transliteration with the long-vowel ー on the stressed syllable; no '地区/区' suffix, since the Russian has none.
reasons.\u0441\u0443\u0431\u0431\u043e\u0442\u04: The first-use gloss should say 'Saturdays' because that is what the word literally means and explains the transliteration.
reasons.\u0417\u0430\u0441\u0435\u0434\u0430\u04: Ostap's mock-parliamentary flourish needs the exclamation and the formal 'session'; 'meeting goes on' is too flat.
reasons.\u0421\u0442\u0430\u0440\u043a\u043e\u04: Descriptive name plus acronym as the brief asks; zh taken from candidate 2 because '旧市公用局' mistranslates 'Star-' as 'old'.
reasons.\u041c\u0435\u043b\u044c\u0441\u0442\u04: 'Melstroy' matches the -oy transliteration used elsewhere (Stargorod, Polesov), and 'Mill-Construction Trust' sounds like a real Soviet trust.
reasons.\u043a\u043e\u043d\u0446\u0435\u0441\u04: Two fixed forms for the two Russian words keep the NEP joke; the second candidate's ja collapses them into one term.
reasons.\u0438\u043d\u0432\u0430\u043b\u0438\u04: 'Imperialist War' officialese retained; 残疾 is the current respectful Chinese term, 残废 reads as dated and pejorative.
reasons.\u043e\u0440\u0434\u0435\u0440: 'Allotment order' is one short term that fits every paperwork scene; 'chit' is too casual for a document the plot depends on.
reasons.\u041b\u0435\u0434 \u0442\u0440\u043e\u0: Fixed identical English; 坚冰已破 is proverb-shaped in Chinese and ましたぞ carries Ostap's mock-solemnity.
reasons.\u00ab\u0422\u0440\u0435\u0443\u0433\u04: Keeps the brand name and says it is a rubber works so the galosh ashtray makes sense; 'tyres' is simply wrong.
reasons.\u0434\u0432\u043e\u0440\u043d\u0438\u04: 'Yard-keeper' is the accepted term in Russian-literature English and conveys the quasi-official role better than 'yardman'.
reasons.\u0421\u0442\u0430\u0440\u0433\u043e\u04: Plain transliteration; bundling Gusishche into the entry conflates two places.
reasons.\u043c\u0438\u043b\u0438\u0446\u0438\u04: One-word 'militiaman' book-wide; the parenthetical glosses belong in a single first-use note, not in the fixed term.
reasons.\u0412\u0438\u043a\u0442\u043e\u0440 \u0: 维克托 is the standard Chinese for Виктор and ポレソフ needs no long vowel on an unstressed syllable.
reasons.\u0441\u043b\u0435\u0441\u0430\u0440\u04: He is a mechanic with a workshop, so 'mechanic'/機械工/钳工; 'locksmith'/鍵屋 misreads слесарь.
reasons.\u043e\u0442\u0435\u0446 \u0424\u0435\u0: Only this candidate fixes distinct renderings for the three address forms, which is the whole difficulty; zh reordered to natural name-then-title.
reasons.\u0434\u043e\u043f\u0440: The acronym plus 'prison' in every language keeps the monk/prison pun; bare 強制労働所/强制劳动所 could be read as a workhouse.
reasons.\u0436\u0438\u043b\u043e\u0442\u0434\u04: Capitalised institution with the transliteration once, so the archive plot has a proper-named office; 課/处 match отдел better than 局.
reasons.\u0410\u043b\u044c\u0445\u0435\u043d (\u: Slash form lets the nickname and full name alternate as in the text; 阿尔亨 is closer to Альхен than 阿利欣.
reasons.\u043a\u0440\u0430\u0441\u043d\u044b\u04: First-use gloss 'political reading room' is needed in English too, then 'the Red Corner' stands alone.
reasons.\u0442\u0443\u0430\u043b\u044c\u0434\u04: 'Calico' reads instantly as cheap cotton and yields a workable 'calico palace' for the чертог joke; the loanword would need a note.
reasons.\u0432\u0435\u043b\u0438\u043a\u0438\u04: 'The Grand Strategist' is the rendering English readers know from the standard translation; ja/zh candidates agree.
reasons.\u041a\u043b\u0430\u0432\u0434\u0438\u04: イヴァーノヴナ keeps the ヴ convention used for every other name in this glossary (ヴィクトル, ヴォロビャニノフ).
reasons.\u0434\u0435\u043b\u043e\u043f\u0440\u04: 'Civil registry office' tells the reader what ZAGS is; 'records clerk' keeps the humble rank that makes the bathos.
reasons.\u0421\u0442\u0430\u0440\u043e\u043f\u04: 斯卡娅 is the standard Chinese for the feminine -ская ending.
reasons.\u0433\u0440\u043e\u0431\u043e\u0432\u04: 'Master of the coffin trade' keeps the guild pomposity; 棺材铺掌柜 preserves that he keeps a shop, and ベゼンチューク marks the stressed syllable.
reasons.\u0443\u0435\u0437\u0434\u043d\u044b\u04: 'District town' and 县城 are the accepted equivalents of уездный город; N郡の町 avoids inventing a 郡都 rank.
reasons.\u0443\u0438\u0441\u043f\u043e\u043b\u04: Capitalised committee name reads as an institution and 'State Plate No. 1'/国字第一号 makes the mark-of-power joke explicit.
reasons.\u0433\u043e\u0441\u043f\u043e\u0434\u04: The pair must be господин/товарищ, so the ruling states both words; 旦那 and 老爷 mark the old-regime tradesman's deference that 様/先生 lose.
reasons.\u0446\u0435\u0440\u043a\u043e\u0432\u04: Folk forms without 'St' carry the provincial flavour the brief wants; 和 is the plainer Chinese conjunction.
reasons.\u0418\u043f\u043f\u043e\u043b\u0438\u04: Bare full name with the ヴォロビャニノフ spelling already used in the господин entry; alternation by surname or name-patronymic follows the Russian without a note.
reasons.\u0442\u0443\u0434\u044b \u0435\u0435 \u: The absurd 'swing' must survive in all three languages as a fixed formula; ちくしょうめ and 见他的鬼去 are ordinary curses.

value.term: «Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» / «Запорожцы пишут письмо султану»
value.finding: In ch. 5 Bender considers offering the Stargorod children's commission (Стардеткомиссия) the rights to a still-unpainted picture, 'The Bolsheviks Write a Letter to Chamberlain', modelled on Repin's 'Zaporozhian Cossacks Write a Letter to the Sultan' (Russian Museum, 1880–91; English title 'Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks'), which every Russian knew: a crowd of laughing Cossacks dictating an obscene refusal to the Turkish sultan's demand of submission. The joke is topical: on 23 Feb 1927 British Foreign Secretary Austen Chamberlain sent a note demanding the USSR stop anti-British propaganda; Pravda answered with 'Our answer to Chamberlain' (2 Mar 1927), Britain broke off relations in May after the ARCOS raid, and the slogan became a nationwide poster/fund-raising campaign (Osoaviakhim air squadron 'Our answer to Chamberlain'), so Chamberlain was the stock villain of 1927 cartoons. Bender's idea is even second-hand: Krasny Perets no. 6 (1923) had already printed 'The Bolsheviks Write a Reply to the English Curzon' with Kalinin, Chicherin, Trotsky, Stalin etc. in the Cossacks' poses. Kalinin (head of state, 'all-Union elder') and Chicherin (foreign commissar) are the leaders whose costumes Bender worries about; the phrase 'наш ответ Чемберлену' survives in Russian as an ironic idiom for a blustering 'worthy reply'. The Richardson English translation renders it 'The Bolsheviks Answer Chamberlain' after 'The Zaporozhe Cossacks Answer the Sultan'.

value.term: «Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» / «Запорожцы пишут письмо султану»
value.finding: In ch. 5 Bender considers selling the Stargorod children's commission a not-yet-painted picture, 'The Bolsheviks Write a Letter to Chamberlain', modelled on Repin's 'Zaporozhtsy' (1880–91), popularly known as 'The Zaporozhian Cossacks Write a Letter to the Turkish Sultan': a crowd of laughing Cossacks composing an obscenely defiant reply to the Sultan's demand of surrender, one of the best-known images in Russia. The topical hook is the 1927 crisis with Britain: on 23 Feb 1927 Foreign Secretary Austen Chamberlain sent the USSR a note demanding an end to 'anti-British propaganda'; Pravda answered on 27 Feb and 2 Mar with 'Our answer to Chamberlain', which became the slogan of a mass campaign of posters, May Day placards, an Osoaviakhim air-fleet fund (9 Jun 1927) and a named squadron and tank column, and Chamberlain became the stock villain of Soviet caricature. The joke had a real prototype: Krasny Perets no. 6 (1923) printed 'The Bolsheviks Write a Reply to the British Curzon', Soviet leaders (Kalinin, Chicherin, Stalin, Trotsky et al.) in Repin's poses, and Krokodil ran 'Workers Write a Reply to Chamberlain' in 1927. Bender's worry about painting Kalinin (nominal head of state) in a papakha and Chicherin (Foreign Commissar) stripped to the waist is what the reader laughs at. Richardson's English renders it 'The Bolsheviks Answer Chamberlain' / 'The Zaporozhe Cossacks Answer the Sultan'; the standard Chinese titles of the painting use 查波罗什人 and 土耳其苏丹, the Japanese Wikipedia title is トルコのスルタンへ手紙を書くザポロージャ・コサック. Note the LibreTexts reader wrongly glosses Chamberlain as Neville; it is Austen.

value.finding: Bortniansky's hymn (1794, words by Kheraskov, after a psalm), used as the unofficial state anthem of the Russian Empire before 'Боже, Царя храни' (1833), and thereafter still the tune the Kremlin's Spasskaya Tower chimes played from 1856 until October 1917; it was then the official hymn of the White armies (1918–23) and of the émigré community. For a Soviet reader in 1928 it was therefore not a random church piece but the sound of the old regime and the Whites, which is why a NEP-era fire extinguisher 'Эклер' hissing this melody (Chapter VIII, the old women's home) is a joke of misplaced loyalties. Sources give no Soviet ban, but the association with tsarism and emigration was live. Established renderings: English 'How Glorious Is Our Lord in Zion' (en.wikipedia, recordings); Chinese 吾主在锡安是何等光荣 (zh.wikipedia article title); Japanese has no article of its own — the Bortniansky page uses the transliteration 『コリ・スラーヴェン』 and Russia Beyond uses 「シオンのわれらが主の何と輝かしき」. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte and '2013' does not apply; the book is 1928.

value.finding: «Быстроупак» is a fictional private packing office in Stargorod: in chapter X it 'announces itself to respected citizen-customers with a black sign with round gold letters' next to the bagel artel, its 'молодцы' (toughs) help the militiaman and later queue for flour, and in chapter XIV its owner Дядьев, a former textile merchant and NEP businessman, is fleeced by Bender's 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare'. The name is a mock Soviet-style clipped compound (быстро + упаковка), the same pattern as real 1920s abbreviations (Хлебопродукт, Москвошвея), and Ilf recorded it in his 1927 notebook simply as 'Упаковочная контора «Быстроупак»' alongside 'Пивная «Вавилон»', i.e. as a specimen of absurd NEP-era shop names. For a Russian reader it connotes a small private nepman firm dressed in bureaucratic-sounding branding; it is not a proverbial phrase. John Richardson's English translation (1961, the standard text online) renders it 'Fastpack' throughout ('the Fastpack packing office', 'young toughs from Fastpack', 'Dyadyev, owner of Fastpack'). Search did not surface the Chinese (张佩文 2004; 白桦熊 2022) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) renderings; those are not verified.

value.note_for_reader: Быстроупак: 'quick' + 'packing', a parody of the clipped compound names Soviet firms and offices adopted in the 1920s; here a small private packing firm owned by the nepman Dyadyev.
value.rationale: The calque ('Fastpack'/快包/速包) keeps the denotation and the joke of a bureaucratic portmanteau on a shop sign, and in English follows Richardson's established rendering; what is given up is the Russian sound and the exact Soviet-acronym flavour, which the side-by-side Russian line and a one-time note restore, so the transliteration is kept only in Japanese where katakana names are conventional.

value.finding: Огонёк (literally 'little flame/light') is a real Moscow illustrated weekly: founded in St Petersburg on 21 December 1899 as a supplement to Birzhevye vedomosti, closed in 1918, and revived in Moscow on 1 April 1923 by the journalist Mikhail Koltsov as 'a Soviet magazine with the old name'. In the NEP years it was the mass-market general-interest picture weekly (photo essays, popular science, celebrities; circulation reportedly around half a million by 1925), which is exactly why a provincial barber in Stargorod would keep it on his table and mine it for 'medical' facts. Ilf and Petrov themselves later wrote for it, so the joke is affectionate: the magazine stands for cheap urban modernity as digested in the provinces. It became a perestroika icon under Korotich (4.6 million copies in 1990), passed to Kommersant in 2009, and ceased print in December 2020; a reader in 2013 knew it as a still-running, slightly old-fashioned national institution. The novel's passage (Part I, ch. 2) is rendered by John Richardson as 'the Moscow magazine Ogonyok'; Chinese coverage uses 《星火》 (zh.wikipedia, Russia Beyond Chinese); Japanese uses katakana オゴニョーク (ja.wikipedia, Russia Beyond Japanese, Kotobank). The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte does not apply to this term.

value.finding: A hymn composed by Dmitry Bortniansky in spring 1794 to words by Mikhail Kheraskov (a paraphrase of a psalm, originally a Masonic lodge hymn). It served as the unofficial anthem of the Russian Empire from the reign of Paul I until 'God Save the Tsar' displaced it in the 1830s, and from 1856 to October 1917 the Spasskaya Tower chimes in the Kremlin played it, so for anyone alive in 1928 it was the sound of the old regime; it was briefly revived by the Whites in 1918-20 and has been Russia's military funeral hymn since 2007. In chapter VIII the 'Eclair' foam extinguisher that Alkhen has gutted for parts emits, instead of foam, 'a thin hissing reminiscent of the old-time melody' of this hymn: a tsarist anthem wheezing out of a Soviet old people's home is the joke. Richardson's standard English translation (1961) renders it 'the ancient hymn "How Glorious Is Our Lord on Zion"'; English Wikipedia's title is 'How Glorious Is Our Lord in Zion'; Chinese Wikipedia titles it 《吾主在锡安是何等光荣》 and calls it the empire's 非正式颂歌; Japanese Wikipedia's anthem list gives 「シオンにおわす我らが主は何と偉大かな」 for 1794-1816 and 1918-20. I could not verify how the published Chinese (张佩文, 2004) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) translations of the novel handle the line.

Sources give no Soviet ban, but the association with tsarism and emigration was live. value.finding: Огонёк (literally 'little flame/light') is a real Moscow illustrated weekly: founded in St Petersburg on 21 December 1899 as a supplement to Birzhevye vedomosti, closed in 1918, and revived in Moscow on 1 April 1923 by the journalist Mikhail Koltsov as 'a Soviet magazine with the old name'. In the NEP years it was the mass-market general-interest picture weekly (photo essays, popular science, celebrities; circulation reportedly around half a million by 1925), which is exactly why a provincial barber in Stargorod would keep it on his table and mine it for 'medical' facts. Ilf and Petrov themselves later wrote for it, so the joke is affectionate: the magazine stands for cheap urban modernity as digested in the provinces. It became a perestroika icon under Korotich (4.6 million copies in 1990), passed to Kommersant in 2009, and ceased print in December 2020; a reader in 2013 knew it as a still-running, slightly old-fashioned national institution. The novel's passage (Part I, ch. 2) is rendered by John Richardson as 'the Moscow magazine Ogonyok'; Chinese coverage uses 《星火》 (zh.wikipedia, Russia Beyond Chinese); Japanese uses katakana オゴニョーク (ja.wikipedia, Russia Beyond Japanese, Kotobank). The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte does not apply to this term.

In the 1920s it was the mass-circulation Soviet picture weekly (photos, popular science, fiction, current events), a lowbrow-respectable magazine found in barbershops and waiting rooms; it later reached 4.6 million copies under Vitaly Korotich in the glasnost era and ceased print publication in December 2020 under Kommersant. In the novel (Part 1, ch. 2) the barber 'Pierre and Constantine', alias Andrei Ivanovich, airs his medical knowledge 'почерпнутые им из московского журнала «Огонек»', which lies on his table 'для услаждения бреющихся граждан' — the joke is a provincial barber retailing half-digested popular-science snippets as expertise. value.finding: The narrator's tag for Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov in ch. X ('Слесарь, попугай и гадалка'): he is introduced at the well as 'соседом Виктором Михайловичем Полесовым, слесарем-интеллигентом', later 'гениальный слесарь-интеллигент', 'кустарь-одиночка с мотором' (an actual 1920s tax/statistics category for a self-employed artisan with a machine, listed as a catchphrase in the Большой словарь цитат, ch. 14) and 'со средним образованием'; he is 'кипучий лентяй', a fussy know-all who never finishes a job and later becomes the 'conspiracy' hothead. Слесарь here is a fitter/metalworker who runs a repair shop and fixes gates and engines, not a locksmith. Интеллигент is the pre-revolutionary social type (educated, opinionated, given to talk rather than work), and welding it to a workman's trade is an oxymoron: the mockery is that a semi-educated artisan poses as a member of the intelligentsia, which is exactly the type the Soviet 1920s sneered at. The phrase is still quoted in Russian as a jibe (e.g. blog posts applying it to public figures). Existing renderings: English reviews and summaries of the Richardson/Fisher translations use 'the mechanic intellectual' / 'an intellectual mechanic'; the standard Chinese translation (张佩文, 人民文学出版社, 2004) has '天才的知识分子钳工'; 江川卓's Japanese translation (筑摩書房, 1969) could not be checked online. The prompt's mention of 'around 2013' and 'Durov and VKontakte' does not apply to this 1928 term and was disregarded.

value.finding: It is the coffin-maker Bezenchuk's signature filler-oath in chapter 1 of The Twelve Chairs (1928): 'туды' is sub-standard for 'туда' (thither), and the whole thing is a euphemised regional curse of the 'туды твою мать' family with the obscene noun swapped for the absurd 'качель' (swing; dialect 'качалка'). The Big Dictionary of Russian Sayings (Mokienko & Nikitina 2003, citing Podyukov 1989) lists 'туды (растуды) твою/вашу/его качель!' as prost., obl., bran.: a curse ('may you perish') or an expression of extreme annoyance; Russian readers today know it almost entirely through Bezenchuk and quote it as a jokey 'to hell with it', with folk accounts saying Ilf and Petrov picked it up from yard-keepers' or Odessa speech. John Richardson's 1961 English translation flattens it to a recurring 'durn it' ('Does the Nymph, durn it, really give good service?'); Anne Fisher's 2011 translation could not be checked, and no Chinese (Zhang Peiwen 2004, Xu Changhan 2022) or Japanese (Egawa Taku 1966/69) rendering was found online. The brief's mention of Durov, VKontakte and 2013 is template noise and does not apply to this term.

value.finding: A sub-standard euphemistic oath: 'туды' is dialect for 'туда' ('over there'), and 'качель' (swing) is a nonsense stand-in for the obscene noun that would normally end a curse of the 'туды его в...' / 'чтоб тебя...' type; Russian dictionaries and Q&A sites describe it as просторечие that replaces мат to express irritation or dismissal, comparable to 'туды через коромысло'. It is known to Russians almost entirely as Bezenchuk the coffin-maker's catchphrase in The Twelve Chairs (ch. 1-2: 'Нимфа, туды ее в качель, разве товар дает?'; 'кисть жидкая, туды ее в качель'; 'Живая! Туды ее в качель!'), made proverbial by Rolan Bykov's delivery in the 1976 film; it is a fixed formula, not a fresh curse, and its humour lies in the absurd swing. Existing renderings: John Richardson's English uses 'durn it', Anne O. Fisher's 2011 translation 'dadgum it' (both minced rural oaths, swing dropped); Zhang Peiwen's Chinese uses a context-adapted '去他们的吧' rather than a fixed formula; no Japanese rendering (Egawa Taku, 1961) could be verified online.

value.finding: A milítsioner is a rank-and-file officer of the milítsiya, the Soviet civil police. The name was adopted by the Provisional Government's decree of 17 April 1917 and reaffirmed by the Bolsheviks on 10 November 1917 as the 'Workers' and Peasants' Militsiya', deliberately chosen to tie the new force to popular self-organisation and to disown the tsarist 'politsiya'; the word survived until Russia restored 'politsiya' on 1 March 2011. In 1928 it therefore carried a distinctly new-regime flavour: a milítsioner is the ordinary street cop of NEP Russia, a figure of mild comedy rather than fear (the terror organs were the OGPU, not the militsiya), and the narrators use him as a stock piece of Soviet street furniture. John Richardson's English translation (the widely circulated 1961/1965 text) renders the institution as 'the Soviet militia' in explicit contrast to 'the tsarist police'; Japanese reference usage is 民警 (ミリツィヤ) for the Soviet-era force versus 警察 for post-2011; Chinese Wikipedia titles the force 苏联民兵 but records 民警 as the standard alternative, and in Chinese everyday usage 民警 also denotes an ordinary uniformed officer of the PRC's 人民警察, which makes it read naturally. The prompt's references to 2013, Durov and VKontakte do not apply to this 1928 term and were disregarded.

value.finding: Жилотдел is the standard early-Soviet abbreviation of жилищный отдел, the housing department attached to the executive committee of a local Soviet; dictionaries of Soviet usage define it as the office that 'kept account of and distributed living space' (учёт и распределение жилой площади). In 1918–1921 these departments (and their district housing councils/commissions) carried out the requisition of 'bourgeois' flats and movable property under decrees such as the Moscow Soviet's 11 Sept 1918 order 'О порядке реквизиции жилых помещений и движимого имущества', issuing the ордера (allocation warrants) by which rooms and furniture were assigned — the very papers Ostap buys from Korobeinikov. In the novel the term is concrete and load-bearing: all Vorobyaninov's furniture 'в 1919 году увезли в жилотдел' (ch. VII); the building 'раньше была здесь женская гимназия, а потом жилотдел' (ch. X); 'жилотдел был расформирован в 1921 году и... обширный его архив слит с архивом Старкомхоза' (ch. XI); one chair went to Gritsatsuev 'по резолюции завжилотделом т. Буркина'. For a 1928 (and still a 2013) Russian reader it connotes War-Communism confiscation and уплотнение, a dead institution whose paperwork outlived it, and the deadpan officialese of the ордер. Existing renderings: Richardson's English (lib.ru) uses 'the housing division' throughout and 'Stargorod communal services' for Старкомхоз; Fisher's 2011 text could not be checked online; a Chinese retelling of the plot uses 住宅管理科 for the 1919 confiscation, and Xu Changhan's 2022 translation and Egawa Taku's 1969 Japanese translation (十二の椅子, 筑摩書房) exist but their wording for this term was not retrievable, so no established zh/ja rendering is confirmed.
sources: https://www.amazon.co.jp/十二の椅子-1969年-イリヤ・イリフ/dp/B000J94TF4

value.finding: Жилотдел is the War-Communism-era clipped name for the жилищный отдел, the housing department of a city or district soviet executive committee (исполком): the office that, under the December 1917 SNK/NKVD decrees on municipalising housing and the 1918 Moscow-soviet rules on requisitioning dwellings and movable property, evicted or 'compacted' (уплотнение) bourgeois households and issued ордера (written orders) allocating their rooms and furniture to workers and institutions. By the SNK statute of 8 April 1920 'жилищное дело' passed to the new коммунальные отделы of the исполкомы, and with NEP and the 1921 demunicipalisation decree the separate housing departments were wound up, which is exactly what the novel records: 'жилотдел был расформирован в 1921 году и... архив слит с архивом Старкомхоза' (ch. XI); Tikhon says 'всю мебель в 1919 году увезли в жилотдел' (ch. VII), and Korobeinikov's stolen copies of its ордера are what the whole hunt runs on. For a 1928 reader the word carried the smell of 1918-21 — requisition, communal-flat 'compaction', a defunct office whose paper still decides who owns what; by 2013 it reads as a dead Soviet bureaucratic abbreviation, one of the novel's period 'sovietisms', with a faint comic note that its own sofa sits in the hall with the upholstery ruined. The gloss's claim that it occupied the girls' school is not in the canonical text (chs. VII, XI, XII checked); the text only says 'тот дом, в котором когда-то был жилотдел'. Existing English translations (Richardson 1961, and per search snippets Fisher 2011) render it 'housing division'; no published Chinese (张佩文 2004, 白桦熊 2021) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) rendering could be verified online.

value.finding: In chapter I of the novel the phrase names the parish of Father Fyodor Vostrikov: 'священник церкви Фрола и Лавра, отец Федор', in the county town of N (Stargorod). Flor and Lavr (Latin Florus and Laurus) are 2nd-century Illyrian martyr-stonemasons whose feast (18/31 August) became the Russian peasant 'horse holiday'; in folk speech and church dedications they are Frol and Lavr (or Lavyor), the 'лошадники', and hundreds of provincial Russian churches bore the name. value.finding: The church where Father Fyodor Vostrikov is priest in the town of N (opening sentence of Chapter III: «священник церкви Фрола и Лавра, отец Федор Востриков»). It is dedicated to the 2nd-century Illyrian martyrs Florus and Laurus (Флор и Лавр, feast 18/31 August), who in Russian folk religion were the patron saints of horses; 'Фрол' is the peasant, vernacular form of the church-Slavonic 'Флор' (Tolstoy's War and Peace has the same 'лошадиный праздник Фрола и Лавра', and 'Фролов день' was the horse holiday). Such dedications were common in Russian towns (Uglich, several Moscow churches), so to a Russian reader the name signals a thoroughly ordinary small-town parish church with a rustic, horse-and-cart flavour, which sets up the comedy of its priest's get-rich schemes; the folk form, not the ecclesiastical one, carries that flavour. Existing English: Richardson (1961) 'Church of St. Frol and St. Laurence' (a hybrid; Laurus is not Laurence), Fisher (2011) reported as 'Frol and Lavr Church'; Russia Beyond's Japanese site writes the saints フロルスとラウルス / フロールとラヴル. I could not access the published Chinese (张佩文 2004) or Japanese (江川卓 1966) texts to confirm their renderings, so those remain unverified.

value.finding: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova is Ippolit Matveevich Vorobyaninov's тёща (his late wife Marie's mother), an old provincial noblewoman in Stargorod who dies in chapter II ('Кончина мадам Петуховой') after confessing that she sewed her diamonds into the seat of one of the twelve dining-room chairs; the novel's Part Three is titled 'Сокровище мадам Петуховой'. Chapter I gives her the book's deadpan treatment: 'Ипполит Матвеевич не любил своей тещи. Клавдия Ивановна была глупа... Скупа она была до чрезвычайности... Голос у ней был такой силы и густоты, что ему позавидовал бы Ричард Львиное Сердце', and she is a dreamer of prophetic dreams. The text calls her only 'Клавдия Ивановна', 'теща', 'старуха' or 'мадам Петухова'; the name-plus-patronymic is the ordinary respectful Russian address for an older woman and carries no joke of its own — the comedy is in the narration around her. For a Russian reader she is the stock тёща of Soviet humour (the domineering mother-in-law who knows the family money) and the origin of the whole treasure hunt. The 1961 Richardson English translation (lib.ru) anglicises her as 'Claudia Ivanovna' and uses 'mother-in-law' throughout; a search summary claimed Fisher (2011) does the same but this could not be verified. The 2022 上海译文 Chinese edition (白桦熊) titles chapter II '佩图霍娃太太辞世'; 克拉夫季娅 is the 新华社 standard Chinese for Клавдия. No Japanese source giving the katakana of her name was found (Egawa Takashi's 1966/1969 translation is not online); Japanese summaries call her 義母.

value.finding: «Треугольник» is the Petersburg rubber works on the Obvodny Canal, founded 1859/60 as the Russian-American Rubber Manufactory (ТРАРМ); from 1888 it stamped its galoshes with a triangle so that illiterate buyers could recognise them, took the trade name «Треугольник» officially in 1908, and was renamed «Красный треугольник» after nationalisation (1922). It was the country's near-monopoly galosh maker, supplier to the Imperial court, and in the NEP years the rubber trust advertised heavily (Mayakovsky wrote its slogans), so for a 1928 reader the word meant one thing: galoshes. In ch. XI the swindled archivist Korobeinikov kicks his table and «подпрыгивала пепельница, сделанная на манер калоши с красной надписью «Треугольник»» — a promotional galosh-shaped ashtray, a pun on the firm's product that also fits the petty-bourgeois clutter of his room; the same brand recurs as torn «Треугольник» tyre covers in Bezenchuk's town. Richardson's English (1961) renders it plainly as 'Triangle' ('the clog-shaped ash-tray with the word "Triangle" on it', misreading калоша as clog); English sources on the factory use 'Triangle'/'Red Triangle'. I found no published Chinese or Japanese rendering of this sentence online (the prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte/2013 is a template slip unrelated to this 1928 term).

It was the country's near-monopoly galosh maker, supplier to the Imperial court, and in the NEP years the rubber trust advertised heavily (Mayakovsky wrote its slogans), so for a 1928 reader the word meant one thing: galoshes. In ch. Richardson's English (1961) renders it plainly as 'Triangle' ('the clog-shaped ash-tray with the word "Triangle" on it', misreading калоша as clog); English sources on the factory use 'Triangle'/'Red Triangle'. value.finding: Старгород (Star-gorod, literally 'Old Town') is the fictional provincial town where Part One, «Старгородский лев», is set; its people are старгородцы and its institutions carry the adjective старгородский (Старгородская правда, the 1 May tram line). Ilf and Petrov borrowed the name from Leskov's «Соборяне» (1872), where Stargorod embodies patriarchal old Russia; in the 1928 novel the same name is turned ironic, standing for provincial bustle and NEP-era pretension in a town of pre-revolutionary leftovers. Its real-life prototype is generally held to be Starobelsk (Luhansk region), which the authors visited as Gudok correspondents in 1923; the village Chmarovka from which Ostap arrives is a real Starobelsk suburb. Established renderings: English translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) use 'Stargorod'; Ekawa Takashi's Japanese translation uses スタルゴロド; but the Chinese tradition (Xu Changhan; Bai Huaxiong, Shanghai Translation 2022) calques it as 老城 (Part One: 老城里的狮子), and I found no Chinese edition using a transliteration.

value.rationale: English and Japanese keep the proper-name denotation and the established transliteration (Stargorod / スタルゴロド), giving up the 'Old Town' pun to the one-line note; Chinese follows the established calque 老城, which keeps the meaning and derives cleanly (老城人, 《老城真理报》, 老城电车) at the cost of looking like a common noun beside the transliterated en/ja columns. All derived forms must follow the one choice per language.

value.finding: Старгород ('Old-town', стар- + город) is the invented provincial town where Part One ('Старгородский лев') is set: Vorobyaninov's home, the site of the Second Social Security Home, the 'Союз меча и орала', the newspaper «Старгородская правда» and the tram whose first car runs on 1 May 1927 (ch. XIII: 'первый в Старгороде вагон электрического трамвая', 'старгородцы только отпускали шуточки'). For a Russian reader the name is a mock-generic, Gogolian toponym in the line of Mirgorod and of Leskov's Stargorod in «Соборяне» (ru.wikipedia lists both), i.e. 'any sleepy old provincial town', not a real place; Starobelsk (Luhansk region, visited by Ilf and Petrov for «Гудок» in 1923; Bender monument 2007/2008) is the usual real-life prototype, with Odessa and Shargorod also claimed. Existing renderings: English editions (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011, Wikipedia) transliterate 'Stargorod' and use it attributively ('Stargorod criminal investigation department'); Japanese coverage (Egawa Taku's translation as quoted, RBTH Japan) uses スタルゴロド; but all three Chinese editions found (张佩文 2004 人民文学, 徐昌翰 2022 江苏凤凰, 白桦熊 2022 上海译文) calque it as 老城 ('第一部 老城名流' / '老城里的狮子', '来到了老城'), not 斯塔尔戈罗德. The prompt's mention of 'Durov and VKontakte' and 'around 2013' does not apply to this term.

value.note_for_reader: Старгород, literally 'Old Town', is an invented provincial town in the manner of Gogol's Mirgorod; English and Japanese keep the Russian sound (Stargorod / スタルゴロド), Chinese editions translate the meaning (老城).
value.rationale: en and ja follow the established transliterations of every existing translation (denotation and proper-name status kept, the 'Old Town' pun given up and supplied once in the note); zh follows the calque used by all three published Chinese translations, which keeps the meaning and mock-generic flavour at the cost of a name that looks like a common noun. Derived forms bind mechanically: старгородцы = Stargorod residents / 老城人 / スタルゴロドの住民, «Старгородская правда» = the Stargorod Pravda / 《老城真理报》 / 『スタルゴロド・プラウダ』, старгородский трамвай = the Stargorod tram / 老城电车 / スタルゴロドの市電.

value.finding: A fictional character, not a real person: the Stargorod mechanic of The Twelve Chairs, introduced in the chapter «Слесарь, попугай и гадалка» as «слесарь-интеллигент» and, among the town's «кустари с мотором», the most inept — the narrators' verdict «Это был кипучий лентяй» (Richardson 1961: 'an ebullient idler'). His workshop is full of unfinished jobs; he chatters with the fortune-teller Elena Stanislavovna, longs for the old regime, and Ostap recruits him as the first dupe of the bogus 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare'. For a Russian reader by 2013 he is a stock type — the loud know-it-all bungler — and «кипучий лентяй» is itself a proverbial phrase. The text calls him by surname, by 'Виктор Михайлович' (the polite form, often with mock solemnity) and by 'слесарь'; all three refer to the same man. The two English translations already differ on the first name (Richardson: 'Victor Mikhailovich Polesov'; modern usage and the Fisher-era coverage: 'Viktor'). No attested Chinese or Japanese spelling of the full name was found online; a Chinese reading edition refers to him as 波列索夫, a 钳工.

value.finding: A fictional character, not a historical person: the Stargorod 'слесарь-интеллигент' introduced in chapter X ('Слесарь, попугай и гадалка'), the clumsiest of the town's 'кустари с мотором' (licensed one-man artisans of the NEP years), a 'кипучий лентяй' who abandons every job (the dismantled gate of house no. 5, a home-made motorcycle that runs once and explodes) to meddle in everyone else's, and the monarchist gossip who leads Vorobyaninov to the fortune-teller Elena Stanislavovna and is enrolled by Bender in the sham 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare'. In the source he is named by surname, by name-patronymic, by full name, and by mocking epithets (слесарь-интеллигент, слесарь-механик, слесарь-энтузиаст, 'Витька-слесарь', 'семибатюшная гадюка со средним образованием'). For a Russian reader by 2013 'Полесов' and 'кипучий лентяй' are bywords for the frantic, opinionated busybody who is useless at his own trade; bloggers still use the name that way (2012, 2016). value.finding: A stern placard on the wall of the Stargorod ZAGS (registry office) in chapter I, where Ippolit Matveyevich registers marriages and deaths; it hangs under the wheezing clock and so cows the young groom that, 'although he had not yet begun his business, he already wanted to leave' (Хотя дела своего мужчина в пиджаке еще и не начинал, но уйти ему уже хотелось), before blurting out 'Сочетаться!'. Dushenko's Большой словарь цитат identifies it as a slightly altered version of a real 1920s institutional placard, «Кончил дело — уходи», one of the curt anti-loitering notices (alongside «Без дела не входить», «Соблюдай очередь») that Soviet offices hung for petitioners; Ilf and Petrov reused the wording as the title of a 1932 feuilleton mocking the anonymous author of such 'комхозовские афоризмы'. For a Russian reader it is the voice of NEP-era bureaucratic rudeness, and via the novel it became a catchphrase. Established renderings found: Richardson (1961) 'Finish Your Business and Leave'; the Shanghai Translation (2022, tr. 白桦熊) text surfaced in search as '事情办完——即刻走人' (page itself could not be fetched to confirm); no Japanese wording from Egawa Takashi's translation was findable online.

value.finding: It is the curt placard (плакат/лозунг) in the Stargorod ZAGS where Vorobyaninov clerks (Part I, ch. 1): the office clock hangs 'над лозунгом «Сделал свое дело — и уходи»', and a few lines later the groom in the quilted jacket is cowed by the ink smell, the wheezing clock 'а в особенности строгим плакатом «Сделал свое дело — и уходи»'; the joke follows at once: 'Хотя дела своего мужчина в пиджаке еще и не начинал, но уйти ему уже хотелось' (ZiF 1928 text; later editions 'Молодой человек еще и не начинал своего дела, а уйти ему уже хотелось'). Such peremptory notices were real fixtures of early-Soviet offices, not the authors' invention: Ilf and Petrov's 1932 feuilleton titled 'Сделал свое дело и уходи' (Советское искусство, 2 Feb 1932) catalogues them alongside 'Без дела не входить', 'Не задавай кассиру вопросов', 'Соблюдай очередь', praising their 'молодецкая безапелляционная форма'. To a Russian reader the line carries the bullying tone of petty officialdom toward the visitor (посетитель), and the novel's use made it a quotable tag. The only established published English rendering found is Richardson (1961): 'Finish Your Business and Leave', used identically at both occurrences; Fisher's 2011 wording could not be checked online. No Chinese (张佩文 et al.) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) text of the passage is online, so those renderings are not attested. (The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte and 2013 does not apply to this 1928 term and was ignored.)

value.finding: A subbotnik (from суббота, Saturday) is a day of unpaid collective labour: the first was held on 12 April 1919 by fifteen communists at the Moscow-Kazan railway depot, who worked through the night repairing locomotives; Lenin blessed the practice in 'A Great Beginning' (Pravda, 28 June 1919) as 'the actual beginning of communism', and himself carried logs at the first all-Russian subbotnik in the Kremlin on 1 May 1920. By the NEP years the word already carried a double charge: official heroism-of-labour rhetoric on one side, and on the other the weary, half-ironic memory of mass mobilisations with brass bands that produced little (encyclopedia.com calls them 'a mixture of socialist idealism and coercion'; Russian Life notes that once the fervour faded they became institutionalised and mandatory). This is exactly how the novel uses it: in ch. XIII ('Дышите глубже, вы взволнованы!') the engineer Treukhov recalls that 'в двадцатом году, когда начались субботники, деповцы и канатчики пошли с музыкой на Гусище и весь день копали какие-то ямы' -- holes dug in the wrong place that had to be filled in again -- and later, on the tram-opening platform, 'хотел сказать многое. И про субботники, и про тяжелую работу'. The established renderings are 'subbotnik(s)' in English (Wikipedia, Encyclopedia.com, Russian Life, Marxists.org all keep the loanword), 星期六义务劳动 in Chinese (Baidu Baike lists 共产主义星期六义务劳动 with short form 星期六义务劳动; it is also the everyday press term for present-day Russian subbotniks), and スボートニク in Japanese, glossed 土曜労働 or 勤労奉仕 (ja.wikipedia, RBTH Japan). I could not obtain the Richardson (1961) or Fisher (2011) wording for this passage online; the lib.ru text fetched only reaches chapter 7. Note: the brief's line about 'Durov and VKontakte ... around 2013' does not apply to this term or this book and was ignored.

value.term: «Летопись войны 1914 года» / «Русский паломник» / «История раскола» / нижние чины / Перемышль
value.finding: All are real. In ch. 3 Father Fyodor's tin-bound trunk is lined with pictures cut from «Летопись войны 1914 года», the official illustrated war weekly edited by Maj.-Gen. D. N. Dubensky (Petrograd 1914–17, 132 issues), with the captions «Взятие Перемышля» and «Раздача теплых вещей нижним чинам на позициях»; inside lie a 1903 run of «Русский паломник», the mass-market Orthodox illustrated weekly (1885–1917, publisher P. P. Soikin, begun with John of Kronstadt's blessing), and «История раскола», i.e. Metropolitan Makary's standard seminary text on the 17th-century Old Believer schism (1855). «Нижние чины» is the imperial-army category for privates and NCOs as opposed to officers; Przemyśl (Russian Перемышль) is the Austro-Hungarian fortress that surrendered to Russia on 9/22 March 1915, the great patriotic headline of that spring. For a 1928 reader the set is a deadpan inventory of a provincial priest's dead pre-revolutionary world: loyalist war propaganda, pious reading, and seminary theology, now the wrapping for a get-rich scheme. Richardson's 1961 English gives 'Chronicle of the 1914 War', 'The Capture of Peremyshl', 'Distribution of Comforts to Other Ranks', 'Russian Pilgrim', 'History of the Schism'; Chinese and Japanese book translations are not online, but zh/ja Wikipedia fix the place name as 普热梅希尔 / プシェムィシル and the schism as 教会分裂 / 教会分裂 (古儀式派).

value.finding: The unnamed 'district town of N' of the opening chapter (Bezenchuk and the 'Nymph'); the manuscript shows the town was later merged into Stargorod. 'Город N' is a stock fictional toponym of Russian literature for a provincial backwater (Gogol's Revizor and Dead Souls, Chekhov, Turgenev, Dostoevsky), and N is a placeholder variable, not an initial: the forms 'NN' and 'Энск' exist alongside it. 'Уездный' marks the seat of an uezd, the second-level pre-1917 administrative unit (Wiktionary: 'uyezd town, district town, county town'); the Soviet reform of 1923–1929 replaced uezds with raions, so in 1928 the word was already faintly old-regime and provincial. For a Russian reader the phrase signals from the first line 'this is a Gogol/Chekhov provincial nowhere, treated with mock solemnity'. Published renderings: Richardson (1961) 'the regional centre of N.', Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'the provincial town of N'; 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺, 2022) 'N县城'; no Japanese text of 江川卓's translation (筑摩書房 1969 / 集英社 1966) could be verified online.

value.rationale: All three keep the bare letter N (the Gogol convention) and a small-town denotation: English 'district town' is the dictionary rendering of уездный город and keeps it distinct from Gogol's 'provincial (губернский) town'; Chinese N县城 is the published rendering and 县 maps uezd well; Japanese N市 follows how Gogol's and Chekhov's N is conventionally rendered but gives up the 'uezd' nuance, since 郡 in Japanese has no town-seat sense and 'N郡の町' misreads N as the district's name. The mock-solemn register is left to the sentence around it.

value.finding: «Город N» (also «уездный город N», «губернский город N») is a stock fictional toponym of Russian literature, established by Gogol (The Inspector General, Dead Souls) and continued by Herzen, Turgenev, Dostoevsky, Chekhov and Ilf and Petrov; it denotes a generic provincial backwater standing for all such towns, and the 'N' is a placeholder, not an initial to be expanded. «Уездный» marks the pre-revolutionary уезд, the lowest administrative tier under a губерния: the seat of a rural district, far from any authority, small, stagnant and petty. Fisher (2011) 'the provincial town of N.', Zhang Peiwen's standard Chinese version (人民文学出版社) 'N县城', and Japanese renderings of Gogol's town conventionally use 'N市'; I could not verify the wording of Ekawa Takashi's 1969 Japanese translation of Ilf and Petrov.

value.finding: In Chapter V ('Великий комбинатор') Bender frames the chair hunt as a business deal: 'как непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела, получаю шестьдесят процентов', and from then on the narrator calls the pair 'концессионеры' and their venture 'концессионное предприятие' (e.g. Chapter XXXIX: 'Повеселевшие концессионеры пошли быстрее'; 'членов-пайщиков концессионного предприятия'). A концессия in 1928 was a precise NEP-era legal institution: under Lenin's decree of 23 Nov 1920 foreign firms (Harriman, Lena Goldfields, German and Japanese companies) got temporary usufruct rights to run state-owned assets for profit; there were 103 such concessions at the 1926 peak and most were annulled by the SNK decree of 27 Dec 1930. To a 1928 reader the word carried newspaper-headline weight: foreign capital, big money, official contracts and a whiff of suspicion; applied to two men chasing chairs it is mock-solemn bureaucratic inflation, and the recurring 60/40 renegotiations keep the joke alive. Both published English translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) use 'the concessionaires'. I could not verify the exact wording used in the published Chinese (白桦熊, 上海译文 2022) or Japanese (江川卓, 筑摩書房 1969) translations; for the historical institution Chinese sources use 租让/租让制/租让企业 and Japanese sources use 利権 or コンセッション.

value.finding: A концессия in 1920s Soviet usage was a specific legal institution of NEP: under Lenin's decree of 23 Nov 1920 the state leased mines, oil fields, forests and factories to foreign capitalists (Harriman's manganese, Lena Goldfields, Japanese Sakhalin oil), supervised from 1923 by Glavkontsesskom; there were at most 103 active concessions (1926) and they were wound up after Dec 1930. In chapter VI Bender, negotiating his share, calls himself 'непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела', and the narrator immediately adopts the word ('своему новому компаньону и непосредственному участнику концессии'); thereafter 'концессионеры' is the narrator's fixed mock-official label for the pair, and Ilf and Petrov reuse it in The Golden Calf. For a 1928 reader the joke was that two shabby private treasure-hunters styled themselves after the foreign firms the newspapers wrote about with suspicion; the word was pompous, faintly disreputable and unmistakably NEP. Richardson's English (1961, lib.ru) uses 'concession' / 'the concessionaires' throughout and this has become the standard English label. Egawa Taku's Japanese translation (1969) makes the pair form a 共同利権会社, so 利権 is the established Japanese key; Japanese historiography uses both 利権 and コンセッション for Soviet NEP concessions (北樺太石油コンセッション). Zhang Peiwen's Chinese translation renders Bender's line with 合同 and 合伙人, dropping the institution; Chinese Soviet-history writing calls NEP concessions 租让制 / 租让企业, whereas 特许经营 today means commercial franchising.

rendering.ja: 利権事業者たち（концессия = 利権事業）

value.note_for_reader: Концессия: under NEP the Soviet state leased mines, forests and factories to foreign capitalists as 'concessions'; Bender borrows the official term for a two-man treasure hunt, and the narrator keeps calling the pair 'the concessionaires' ever after.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (an NEP foreign-capital concession) and the mock-official register, binding one fixed label for the whole book with a single note; en follows the established Richardson rendering, ja follows Egawa's 利権 and the historians' term, zh gives up the accepted-but-misleading 特许经营 (modern franchising) for the Soviet-history term 租让, which is less familiar to a lay reader and so leans on the note.

value.finding: In the Russian Empire the дворник was the yard-and-street keeper of an apartment house who was also formally enrolled in the police system: after the 1866 attempt on Alexander II dvorniki were made auxiliaries of the MVD, wore a numbered brass badge and carried a whistle to summon the городовой, kept night watch at the gate, registered tenants and their passports, detained beggars and suspicious persons, and served as witnesses at searches, all under the околоточный надзиратель. After 1917 the political and record-keeping side passed to the управдом and housing committee, and the dvornik was left 'with shovel, scraper and broom', but in the NEP 1920s the habit of petty authority over the yard survived, which is exactly the joke in Chapter XIV: the dvornik of house No. 5 whom Polesov calls 'a boor who has got above himself' chases him down the street and beats him while Polesov shouts 'караул!'. In English coverage the word is rendered 'janitor' (Russia Beyond), 'caretaker' (Richardson's 1961 translation), 'street cleaner' (IMDb credits for Tikhon in the 1971 film) and, in Russianist usage, 'yard-keeper'; Fisher's 2011 translation appears to keep 'dvornik', but I could not verify this from the text. I could not verify how the 上海译文 Chinese or the 江川卓 (筑摩書房 1969) Japanese translations render it: the Chinese e-texts were blocked and the Japanese reviews found do not mention Tikhon. 庭番 is the customary rendering in Japanese Dostoevsky translations and 看院人/扫院人 the customary Chinese ones; neither could be confirmed for this book.

rendering.ja: 庭番

value.note_for_reader: A dvornik kept the yard and pavement of an apartment house and, since tsarist times, doubled as the police's man on the block, with badge and whistle; the habit of authority outlived the Revolution.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a man who keeps the yard, not a US-style indoor janitor) and the 'keeping/watching' element that lets the Polesov chase read as an official throwing his weight around, and each is the established Russianist rendering rather than a coinage; the specific tsarist police connotation cannot be carried by any single word and is handed to the one-line note, while the register stays neutral so the narrators' deadpan does the ironic work.

value.finding: In the Russian Empire the дворник was the yard-and-street keeper of an apartment house who was also formally enrolled in the police system: after the 1866 attempt on Alexander II dvorniki were made auxiliaries of the MVD, wore a numbered brass badge and carried a whistle to summon the городовой, kept night watch at the gate, registered tenants and their passports, detained beggars and suspicious persons, and served as witnesses at searches, all under the околоточный надзиратель. After 1917 the political and record-keeping side passed to the управдом and housing committee, and the dvornik was left 'with shovel, scraper and broom', but in the NEP 1920s the habit of petty authority over the yard survived, which is exactly the joke in Chapter XIV: the dvornik of house No. 5 whom Polesov calls 'a boor who has got above himself' chases him down the street and beats him while Polesov shouts 'караул!'. In English coverage the word is rendered 'janitor' (Russia Beyond), 'caretaker' (Richardson's 1961 translation), 'street cleaner' (IMDb credits for Tikhon in the 1971 film) and, in Russianist usage, 'yard-keeper'; Fisher's 2011 translation appears to keep 'dvornik', but I could not verify this from the text. I could not verify how the 上海译文 Chinese or the 江川卓 (筑摩書房 1969) Japanese translations render it: the Chinese e-texts were blocked and the Japanese reviews found do not mention Tikhon. 庭番 is the customary rendering in Japanese Dostoevsky translations and 看院人/扫院人 the customary Chinese ones; neither could be confirmed for this book.

value.finding: A dvornik was the live-in yard-keeper of a town apartment house: he swept the yard and pavement, locked and unlocked the street gate at night (tenants tipped him a grivennik to be let in — the 'night earnings' the No. 5 dvornik loses when Polesov removes the gates), and, since a decree following the 1866 attempt on Alexander II, served as an unpaid lowest rung of the police: he wore a numbered brass badge, carried a police whistle, checked residence papers, reported suspicious tenants, stood night watch and acted as witness at searches (rules codified 1896). The Kommersant history notes that in 1922 Moscow dvorniks received almost identical orders — report violations, assist the militia, night patrols, whistle and badge — so in 1928 a Russian reader still saw in him a petty, respected-and-feared authority figure, not a mere cleaner; only in the 1960s did he become 'a man with a broom'. Register in the novel is neutral-descriptive, mined for irony (Klavdia Ivanovna dreams of 'dvorniks playing harps'). In chapter X the dvornik of No. 5 does not literally chase Polesov: he comes to demand the gates, begs 'Christ God', utters vague threats, kicks the padlock, tears down Polesov's signboard and raises a public scandal until a militiaman drags him (the dvornik) to the district station — the joke being that the house's own mini-policeman ends up arrested. Existing renderings: Richardson's 1961 English uses 'caretaker' for Tikhon and 'yard-keeper' for exactly this No. 5 dvornik; Wiktionary lists yard-keeper/doorkeeper/caretaker/porter; standard Ru-Zh dictionaries give 看院子的/看院人; Japanese dictionaries give 庭番/管理人/用務員, with 庭番 the conventional choice in Russian-literature translations. I could not verify the Chinese (徐昌翰, 张佩文, 白桦熊) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) editions' wording online.

In 1920s Odessa/NEP speech 'комбинация' meant a clever, usually shady scheme and 'комбинатор' its author (Lechaim traces the formula to Sholem Aleichem's 'человек с комбинациями'); the pompous 'великий' is the authors' irony. value.finding: Старкомхоз is the novel's Soviet-style portmanteau for the Stargorod отдел коммунального хозяйства, the municipal-economy department of the town executive committee (исполком) that ran utilities, housing stock, street upkeep and transport; the real-life generic forms коммунхоз / горкомхоз are attested in the 1998 Dictionary of Soviet-era Language (Mokienko & Nikitina), which cites Ilf and Petrov among its examples. In chapter XIII ('Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!') Gavrilin, 'заведующий Старкомхозом' transferred from Samarkand, sponsors engineer Treukhov's tramway; Treukhov himself is bored in the department's отдел благоустройства mending kerbs and costing poster pillars, and 'грузовики Старкомхоза и Мельстроя' cart children about after the opening. The word carried the flat officialese sound of NEP-era acronym-building (Старгород + коммунальное хозяйство), which the authors exploit for deadpan comedy alongside Мельстрой. The standard English translation (John Richardson, 1961, public-domain text on lib.ru and Fandom) renders Gavrilin as 'chief of the Stargorod communal services', so 'communal services' is the established English wording; Anne Fisher's 2011 rendering could not be verified online, and no Chinese or Japanese published rendering of the term was found in search (Chinese editions by Xu Changhan/Zhang Peiwen and Bai Huaxiong, Japanese by Egawa Taku exist but their text is not indexed).

value.finding: Старкомхоз is a fictional Soviet-style contraction of «Старгородское коммунальное хозяйство», the Stargorod city department of 'communal economy'. In the novel (ch. Гаврилина», Treukhov himself works in its «отдел благоустройства» fixing kerbs and costing poster columns, and «грузовики Старкомхоза» ferry children to the tram opening; in ch. X a craftsman goes «в коммунхоз» to renew a workshop lease, and in ch. VIII Ostap toasts «за ваше коммунальное хозяйство». This mirrors real bodies: after the SNK decree of 8 April 1920 local soviets' коммунотделы/коммунхозы ran water, sewers, trams, housing, land, street improvement and burials under the NKVD's GUKKh, and Moscow's own was abbreviated МКХ (Москоммунхоз). For a 1928 reader the word carried the flavour of clumsy revolutionary acronym-speak and of the shabby, underfunded municipal office where one queued for leases and repairs. The established English rendering (John Richardson, 1961, public-domain text) is 'the Stargorod communal services'; no published Chinese or Japanese rendering could be found online (Chinese and Japanese e-book pages were inaccessible), so zh/ja are decided on the model of the real Soviet institution. value.finding: The narrator's standing epithet for Ostap Bender, first used as the title of the chapter that introduces him (ch. 5/6) and repeated throughout both novels. 'Комбинатор' is not 'combinator': it is a 1920s colloquial word for someone who lives by 'комбинации' — clever, semi-legal arrangements; 'великий' adds a mock-epic, Peter-the-Great grandeur. Russian phrase dictionaries label the expression colloquial, ironic or disapproving: 'a slick rogue who succeeds by elaborate operations, tricks and fraud', and note that it entered the language from the novel; by 2013 it was a proverbial, affectionate label for any charming schemer (a Kharkiv statue is billed as the 'monument to the grand strategist'). English has two established renderings: 'the smooth operator' (Richardson 1961, kept in Fisher's 2009/2011 versions as marketed by Russian Life) and 'the grand strategist' (Gurevich/Anderson, Open Letter 2009; also in tourist and press usage). Chinese: the 2022 Shanghai Translation (Bai Huaxiong) edition titles the chapter '了不起的幕僚'; blurbs call him '大骗子兼冒险家'; no single fixed Chinese epithet is established. Japanese: the 1969 Egawa Taku translation (Chikuma) is not searchable online; Japanese reviews describe Bender as 山師 / 策士 and one gloss gives 偉大なるコンビナートル, so no fixed Japanese phrase could be confirmed.

value.finding: Ostap Bender's signature exclamation, first uttered in the chapter «Бриллиантовый дым» (ch. VI in the canonical text): while Vorobyaninov tells the story of the jewels, Ostap keeps jumping up and shouting it 'to the iron stove', then repeats it when they shake hands on the partnership. «Лёд тронулся» is the spring ice-break on a river (ледоход), used figuratively for 'things have finally started moving, the deadlock is over'; «господа присяжные заседатели» is the address a barrister used to the jury in the pre-revolutionary jury court, abolished in 1917, so in 1928 it is a mock-solemn anachronism, Ostap parodying courtroom oratory to give his swindle comic gravitas (it pairs with his other courtroom tag «Заседание продолжается»). The line became a proverb: Russian media still headline stalled projects that finally move with «Лёд тронулся». English coverage is split: the 1961 Richardson translation has 'Things are moving, gentlemen of the jury', Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation is reported as 'The ice has started breaking up, gentlemen of the jury!', while Wikipedia and Russia Beyond use 'The ice has broken, (ladies and) gentlemen of the jury!'. Published Chinese (张佩文 2004; 白桦熊 2022, whose paratext popularises the sister tag 庭审继续进行) and Japanese (江川卓 1966/1969) renderings of this line could not be retrieved online. The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte coverage is unrelated to this term and was not pursued.

value.finding: An извозчик was a licensed driver of a horse-drawn cab for hire, the ordinary urban taxi of Russian cities before motor transport; the trade split into ломовые (freight carters) and легковые (passenger cabs), and the passenger cabs into cheap peasant 'ваньки', stand-licensed 'биржевые' and expensive 'лихачи'. In 1927 Moscow they were still the everyday way to get across town at night (about 4,900 licensed in 1928, down from ~15,000 before 1917), while motor taxis had only been reintroduced by the Mossovet in December 1924 precisely because cabs, trams and buses were short; by 1934 only 385 remained and the trade was gone by the late 1930s. For a 1928 reader the word carried no exoticism: it was as neutral and daily as 'taxi', with a stock image of a sleepy, grumbling driver on his box, haggling over fares, tipped with a shout of 'Извозчик!' from the pavement. Richardson's 1961 English translation (the text on lib.ru) renders it variously 'cab', 'cabby', 'cab-driver' and, where the horse matters, 'horse-cab' ('His wife took him home in a horse-cab', 'HORSE-CAB NO. 8974'). Japanese has an established equivalent, 辻馬車, used for exactly this Moscow institution by Miyamoto Yuriko in her 1920s essay モスクワの辻馬車, which also transcribes イズヴォシチク and calls the driver 御者. I could not verify online how the Chinese editions (张佩文 2004, 白桦熊 2022) render the word; 马车夫 is the standard dictionary equivalent for a hired-carriage driver in Chinese renderings of Russian literature (e.g. Chekhov's cabman), but I did not confirm it against the Ilf–Petrov text.

rendering.ja: 辻馬車の御者

value.note_for_reader: In 1927 the izvozchik, a horse-drawn cab for hire, was still Moscow's ordinary taxi; motor cabs had only returned in 1924.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a hired horse-drawn cab and its driver, not a taxi) and the plain everyday register, using established forms (Richardson's 'horse-cab', Miyamoto's 辻馬車, dictionary 马车夫); what is given up is the word's total unmarkedness, since 'horse-cab' and 辻馬車 sound faintly period to a modern reader where извозчик did not in 1928. In dialogue the vocative 'Извозчик!' should still go as the short 'Cabby!' / 车夫！ / 御者さん！, with the full rendering kept for narration.

value.finding: In the novel an ордер is the slip issued by the Stargorod housing department (жилотдел) when furniture requisitioned from a private house in 1918-19 was handed to an institution or an individual: chapters XI-XII speak of 'копии ордеров, по которым распределялась изъятая из воробьяниновского особняка мебель', of 'пачки ордеров' on Korobeinikov's shelves, of 'зеленые корешки ордеров' (green counterfoils bearing the recipient's address and signature), and of one 'ордер... на десять стульев, выданный музею мебельного мастерства' and another 'на один стул — т. Грицацуеву'. Ushakov's contemporary dictionary gives the sense exactly: 'письменное предписание, распоряжение' with the examples 'ордер на въезд в новый дом' and 'ордер на обувь' — a state chit entitling the holder to receive a specific scarce thing, the everyday paperwork of requisition and rationing; for a 1928 reader it carried the bureaucratic flavour of the housing 'передел' and уплотнение, not a court order or a purchase order. Both established English translations, Richardson (1961) and Fisher (2011), render it simply as 'orders' ('the orders for the distribution of the furniture requisitioned...', 'bundles of orders... green counterfoils'; Fisher pp. 127-139 'the orders according to which the furniture from V...'). value.finding: Уисполком = уездный исполнительный комитет, the executive committee of the uezd (district) soviet: in 1918-1925 the highest organ of power on the territory of a uezd between congresses of soviets, with its own departments (land, military, finance, police, etc.); the uezd tier was abolished in the 1925-29 regionalisation, so by 1928 the word already sounded provincial and slightly dated. 'Гос. № 1' is a state registration plate of the pre-1931 era, when plates were issued locally and the numbering started at 1; the car of the town's top authority naturally holds plate No. 1. In the novel (Part 1, ch. I and III) it is the single official car of the uezd town N, with 'a tiny radiator and a cumbersome body', which has been stuck for two weeks at the corner of Staropan Square and nearly runs Father Fyodor down; the joke is the pomp of the plate against the wreck that carries it. Existing translations: Richardson (1961, lib.ru) 'the district-executive-committee motor-car, Gos. No. 1'; Anne O. Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'the district executive committee car, Gov't No. 1'; the Shanghai Translation Publishing House Chinese edition '县执行委员会国字1号汽车'. The Egawa Taku Japanese translation (1969/1977) is not online; no Japanese rendering could be verified. The prompt's references to 2013 and to Durov/VKontakte do not apply to this term and were ignored.

value.finding: In the novel this is the state old-women's home in Stargorod, housed in Vorobyaninov's former mansion (the sign Ostap reads in ch. V says «2-й ДОМ СОЦИАЛЬНОГО ОБЕСПЕЧЕНИЯ СТАРГУБСТРАХА»; ch. VIII opens «Завхоз 2-го дома Старсобеса был застенчивый ворюга»), run by the bashful thief Alkhen and filled with his relatives. The gloss's expansion is wrong: Стар- is Старгород, not старость — Старсобес = Старгородский собес (Stargorod social-security office), and соцобес = социальное обеспечение; both spellings name the same institution, and the prototype was a real almshouse (богадельня) on Armyansky Lane in Moscow. For a Russian reader the term connotes a Soviet institutional mouthful of an acronym stuck on an old poorhouse, and after the 1971 and 1976 films 'дом Старсобеса' is shorthand for a shabby, pilfered-from welfare home. Both published English translations already use 'Social Security': Richardson (1961) 'the Second Home of Stargorod Social Security (Administration)', elsewhere 'pensioners' home' / 'old-age pensioners' home'; Fisher (2011) 'the Second Stargorod Social Security Home'. No Chinese (Zhang Peiwen 2004, Bai Huaxiong 2022) or Japanese (Egawa Takashi 1966/1977) rendering of this line could be located online.

value.finding: In the novel an ордер is the slip issued by the Stargorod housing department (жилотдел) when furniture requisitioned from a private house in 1918-19 was handed to an institution or an individual: chapters XI-XII speak of 'копии ордеров, по которым распределялась изъятая из воробьяниновского особняка мебель', of 'пачки ордеров' on Korobeinikov's shelves, of 'зеленые корешки ордеров' (green counterfoils bearing the recipient's address and signature), and of one 'ордер... на десять стульев, выданный музею мебельного мастерства' and another 'на один стул — т. Грицацуеву'. Ushakov's contemporary dictionary gives the sense exactly: 'письменное предписание, распоряжение' with the examples 'ордер на въезд в новый дом' and 'ордер на обувь' — a state chit entitling the holder to receive a specific scarce thing, the everyday paperwork of requisition and rationing; for a 1928 reader it carried the bureaucratic flavour of the housing 'передел' and уплотнение, not a court order or a purchase order. Both established English translations, Richardson (1961) and Fisher (2011), render it simply as 'orders' ('the orders for the distribution of the furniture requisitioned...', 'bundles of orders... green counterfoils'; Fisher pp. 127-139 'the orders according to which the furniture from V...'). I could not reach the text of the Chinese (白桦熊, 上海译文 2022; earlier 张佩文) or Japanese (江川卓, 集英社 1966/1969) translations online, so their renderings are unverified. The prompt's reference to 'Durov and VKontakte, around 2013' does not apply to this 1928 term and was ignored.
