value.finding: Уисполком = уездный исполнительный комитет, the executive committee of the uezd (district) soviet: in 1918-1925 the highest organ of power on the territory of a uezd between congresses of soviets, with its own departments (land, military, finance, police, etc.); the uezd tier was abolished in the 1925-29 regionalisation, so by 1928 the word already sounded provincial and slightly dated. 'Гос. № 1' is a state registration plate of the pre-1931 era, when plates were issued locally and the numbering started at 1; the car of the town's top authority naturally holds plate No. 1. In the novel (Part 1, ch. I and III) it is the single official car of the uezd town N, with 'a tiny radiator and a cumbersome body', which has been stuck for two weeks at the corner of Staropan Square and nearly runs Father Fyodor down; the joke is the pomp of the plate against the wreck that carries it. Existing translations: Richardson (1961, lib.ru) 'the district-executive-committee motor-car, Gos. No. 1'; Anne O. Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'the district executive committee car, Gov't No. 1'; the Shanghai Translation Publishing House Chinese edition '县执行委员会国字1号汽车'. The Egawa Taku Japanese translation (1969/1977) is not online; no Japanese rendering could be verified. The prompt's references to 2013 and to Durov/VKontakte do not apply to this term and were ignored.

value.finding: Туальденор is a Russian trade name from French 'toile du nord' ('cloth of the north'): a plain-weave cotton in which white and black threads are woven together to give a grey colour; denser and stronger than calico, and used for cheap men's shirts, smocks, dressing gowns and work clothes (Andreeva, Fashion Encyclopedia 1997; Orlenko 1996; marked as an obsolete term). In chapter VIII ('Голубой воришка') Ilf and Petrov use it five times for the Stargorod old-women's home — the banner 'A brass band is the path to collective creativity', the old women's dresses 'of the very cheapest mouse-coloured tualdenor', the conductor's grey smock and trousers, the cook's cap and apron, and the fire-extinguisher passage — so that the one drab fabric becomes a running joke about institutional poverty. It is a colourless, matter-of-fact fabric name, not slang, and its comic charge comes from repetition plus the pedantic 'мышиного цвета'. Search did not turn up the wording of the Richardson (1961), Fisher (2011), Chinese, or Japanese editions, so no established target rendering could be verified.

'Calico' was avoided in English because it means printed cotton to American readers.

value.finding: Title of Part I, Chapter XIV (chapter 16 in some editions), where Ostap Bender improvises a secret monarchist 'union' among Stargorod's ex-notables so as to collect 'donations' from them, presenting Vorobyaninov as 'a giant of thought, father of Russian democracy'. The name is a parody of Isaiah 2:4 as it stands in the Church Slavonic/Synodal Bible, 'перекуют мечи свои на орала' (they shall beat their swords into ploughshares): 'орало' is the archaic Slavonic word for a plough, so the name sounds mock-solemn and liturgical while being nonsense, since a pre-revolutionary-style 'Union' named after a peace slogan is absurd (the Soviet state later adopted the very slogan itself, e.g. Vuchetich's 1957 UN statue 'Перекуём мечи на орала'). Wing-word dictionaries record that by the late Soviet and post-Soviet period 'Союз меча и орала' had become a proverbial byword for a sham, paper-only political organisation or conspiracy that exists only in its founders' imagination, and it is still used that way in Russian journalism. Existing translations: Richardson (1961) 'The Alliance of the Sword and Ploughshare'; Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'Sword and Plowshare'; Chinese 张佩文 (人民文学, 2004) '剑犁同盟', 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺, 2022) '剑与犁联合会'; the Japanese 江川卓 translation (1966/1969) is not online and no established Japanese rendering could be found.

rendering.en: The Union of the Sword and the Ploughshare
rendering.ja: 剣と鋤の同盟

value.note_for_reader: A mock name built on Isaiah 2:4, 'they shall beat their swords into ploughshares' (орало is the Church Slavonic word for plough); in Russian it became a byword for a bogus organisation that exists only on paper.
value.rationale: All three renderings keep the denotation (a 'union' of sword and plough) and the biblical echo by using each language's own Bible wording (KJV 'ploughshares', 和合本 '将刀打成犁头'/成语 '铸剑为犁', 新共同訳 '剣を打ち直して鋤とし'), and keep the pompous organisation-name register; what is given up is the Church Slavonic archaism of 'орало' and the ready-made proverbial force the phrase later acquired in Russian, which the note supplies. English and Chinese follow the existing published renderings closely (Richardson's 'Alliance' becomes the more literal 'Union'; Chinese sits between 张佩文's 剑犁同盟 and 徐昌翰's 剑与犁联合会); Japanese is a new rendering since none could be verified.

value.finding: Chapter XIV title and the name of the fictitious monarchist underground Ostap Bender improvises in Stargorod to shake down Vorobyaninov's old-regime acquaintances, presenting Vorobyaninov as a 'giant of thought, father of Russian democracy' and pocketing 'dues' for a non-existent cause. The name parodies Isaiah 2:4 in the Synodal Bible, «перекуют мечи свои на орала» (they shall beat their swords into ploughshares): орало is the Church Slavonic/Synodal word for a plough, so the title yokes a weapon and a peasant tool into a pompous, meaningless emblem. By 2013 it was a fixed крылатое выражение, used ironically of paper organisations and sham alliances that exist only in words. Established renderings: Richardson (1961) 'The Alliance of the Sword and Ploughshare'; Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'The Union of the Sword and the Plowshare'; the 2021 Shanghai Translation edition titles the chapter 「剑犁之盟」. No Japanese rendering of the chapter (Egawa Taku's 1969 十二の椅子) could be verified online; the 新共同訳 Bible renders the verse 「剣を打ち直して鋤とし」, so 鋤 is the word a Japanese reader will recognise.

value.finding: A fictional square in Stargorod, the invented provincial town of Part One. In the 1928 ZiF text it appears in chapter I ('Безенчук и «нимфы»'): the townspeople gossip about Klavdia Ivanovna's illness 'посреди Старопанской площади, у бюстика поэта Жуковского' with the inscription «Поэзия есть бог в святых мечтах земли», and the executive-committee car 'пересек Старопанскую площадь' through the mud; it recurs as the town's main square (the fire brigade drives out of it). value.finding: ЗАГС = (отдел) записи актов гражданского состояния, the civil-registry office created by the Sovnarkom decree of 18 Dec 1917 that took births, marriages and deaths away from the church's metrical books and made them a purely secular, local-soviet paperwork function; by the 1920s a provincial ZAGS was a small office of a head, a few делопроизводители (paper clerks), an archivist and a typist. Делопроизводитель is the lowest desk grade in Soviet office hierarchy: the person who fills in and files the forms. In the novel Ippolit Matveyevich 'служил в загсе, где ведал столом регистрации смертей и браков' (ch. I), and the phrase itself recurs as a narratorial jab — 'В Ипполите Матвеевиче продолжал бушевать делопроизводитель загса' (ch. XX) — so the joke is the ex-marshal of the nobility reduced to the pettiest Soviet clerkship, sitting at a desk 'like an old gravestone' recording deaths. For a Russian reader ZAGS is a byword for drab bureaucratic weddings and death certificates. Existing renderings: Richardson (1961) and Fisher (2011) both use 'registry office' ('he worked in the registry office, where he was in charge of the registration of deaths and marriages'); Chinese summaries of the novel use 县户籍登记处的一名办事员 (Zhang Peiwen tradition); Japanese coverage uses 登記所 (Egawa 1966) or 住民課. I could not open the Chinese or Japanese book texts directly, so the CJK evidence is from summaries and reviews, not the translations themselves.

rendering.en: records clerk at the civil registry office
rendering.ja: 戸籍登録所の書記

value.note_for_reader: ZAGS (загс): the Soviet civil registry that from 1917 replaced church records of births, marriages and deaths — the humblest of desk jobs.
value.rationale: All three keep denotation (a lowly clerk in the secular births-marriages-deaths office) and the bathos of the register; 'civil' is added in English so 'registry office' is not read as land or company registry. Given up: the acronym ZAGS itself and its specifically Soviet flavour, which only the one-line note restores; 户籍 leans toward China's hukou residence system, and 戸籍登録所 is a transparent coinage rather than a real Japanese office, both accepted because they are the renderings Chinese and Japanese readers already meet for this novel.

value.finding: In the novel the word first appears in ch. VI when Ostap fixes his cut: «я, как непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела, получаю шестьдесят процентов»; from ch. VII on the narrator deadpans «концессионеры знали всё» and uses it as the pair's standing name (ru.wikisource ch. VI, VII). The joke is that a con man and an ex-marshal of nobility hunting chairs style themselves after the NEP-era foreign concessions: under Lenin's decree of 23 Nov 1920 and the Главконцесском (1923) the Soviet state leased mines, oilfields and factories to foreign capital (Harriman manganese, Lena Goldfields, Krupp, the Japanese Sakhalin oil concession); they peaked at 103 in 1926 and were being wound down as the book appeared, so for a 1928 reader концессия was fresh newspaper vocabulary meaning a state-sanctioned, slightly suspect deal in which a foreigner extracts profit from Soviet property. Both English translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) keep 'concessionaires' / 'the concession' as the running gag. The 张佩文 Chinese version flattens it to 合伙人 and 合同项目, losing the NEP reference, while Chinese historiography of NEP consistently uses 租让 / 租让制 for these concessions; Japanese coverage of the Soviet concessions of the same years (北樺太石油, 1925 treaty) uses 利権 / 利権契約 / コンセッション. The prompt's reference to Durov and VKontakte around 2013 does not apply to this 1928 term and was disregarded.

rendering.ja: 利権事業者たち / 利権事業

value.note_for_reader: Концессия: a NEP-era lease of state property to a (usually foreign) private operator; Ostap borrows the term to dignify a two-man treasure hunt.
value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a state-granted concession, not a mere partnership) and the mock-official register so the running gag survives; en is the established rendering, zh replaces the proposed 特许经营 (modern franchise/PPP jargon) with the term Chinese NEP historiography actually uses, ja keeps 利権 as the word Japanese sources use for the Soviet concessions of the 1920s. What is given up is the reader's instant sense that this was 1926 headline vocabulary, hence the one-line note at first occurrence.

value.finding: Ostap Bender's recurring catchphrase, first spoken in ch. 6 when he takes charge of the chair hunt ("Спокойно, спокойно. За дело берусь я. Заседание продолжается.") and repeated to his final words in the last chapter, where it is paired with "Лёд тронулся, господа присяжные заседатели". It is the formula of a chairman reopening a session after a disturbance, and Dushenko's dictionary of quotations traces it to a famous 'historical utterance': after the anarchist Vaillant's bomb in the French Chambre des députés on 9 Dec 1893, president Charles Dupuy declared "Messieurs, la séance continue!" — a phrase educated Russians of 1928 knew. Bender uses it, together with 'gentlemen of the jury' (jury trials had been abolished in 1917), as a mock-solemn pre-revolutionary judicial/parliamentary register meaning 'the business goes on, nothing has happened'; Friedberg's reader labels its style юридический. The phrase is now proverbial (in Serov's and Dushenko's dictionaries; a 1976 film song title). Established renderings: Richardson (1961, lib.ru text) uses "The hearing is continued" throughout (last words: "The hearing's continued. Things are moving, gentlemen of the jury"), and a TV Tropes summary of the Fisher 2011 translation gives the same "The hearing is continued!"; the 2022 Chinese edition (江苏凤凰文艺, tr. 徐昌翰) makes "庭审继续进行！" the catchphrase and even titles its editor's note with it. No Japanese rendering (江川卓 tr., 1966/1969) could be located online.

Заседание продолжается.» It recurs to his last words in the book («Заседание продолжается. Лёд тронулся, господа присяжные заседатели»), often paired with the address «господа присяжные заседатели» ('gentlemen of the jury'). The joke is register: заседание is bureaucratic ('session/meeting'), but with the jury address it becomes the mock-solemn voice of a pre-revolutionary trial lawyer — the jury court had been abolished in 1917, so in 1928 it is a dead form Bender revives for effect. It became a proverb meaning 'business as usual, the enterprise goes on despite the setback'. Existing renderings: Richardson (1961, lib.ru) uses 'The hearing is continued' / 'The hearing continues' with 'gentlemen of the jury'; Basharova (2025) 'the meeting continues, ladies and gentlemen of the jury'; the Chinese editions (徐昌翰, 张佩文, 白桦熊/上海译文) all settle on the catchphrase «庭审继续进行！». No Japanese rendering could be verified online (江川卓's 1966/1969 translation is not digitised). The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte coverage appears to be a template error; a search found no use of the phrase by Durov, and the term is anchored in the 1928 novel.

value.finding: Title of the chapter (XIII in the 1928 first-edition numbering, XIV/XV in later editions) in which Stargorod opens its first tram line and a newsreel crew films the ceremony. The phrase is the cameraman-director's stock command, repeated verbatim to everyone he points the lens at: to the engineer Treukhov ('Дышите глубже. Вы взволнованы… Коля! Ноги крупно!'), to the official Gavrilin ('Дышите глубже. Вы взволнованы. Вы никогда прежде не ездили в трамвае'), and to the Komsomol girl Lyuda. The joke is that he dictates the subject's emotion in the flat second-person plural, like a stage direction read aloud; it satirises agitprop newsreel staging and became a Russian catchphrase, used ironically (often attributed loosely to Ostap Bender) to mean 'calm down, you are getting worked up'. Established renderings: Anne O. Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation titles the chapter 'Breathe Deeper, You're Excited!'; Chinese editions have 张佩文 (人民文学 2004) '请做深呼吸：您太激动了！' and 徐昌翰 (后浪) '深呼吸：您是很激动的！'. No text of the Japanese translation (江川卓, 筑摩書房 1969) was findable online, so the Japanese rendering has no located precedent.

rendering.ja: 深く息を吸って——あなたは興奮しているのです！

value.note_for_reader: The newsreel director's stock command to everyone he films; it became a Russian catchphrase for 'calm down, you're getting worked up'.
value.rationale: All three keep the bare imperative plus the flat declarative that assigns the subject his emotion, which is where the humour lives, and the same wording must be reused for each recurrence in the chapter; English adopts Fisher's established title, Chinese drops the softening 请 and 太 of the published versions to keep the deadpan command, Japanese uses のです for the mock-solemn 'explaining' tone since no published Japanese rendering could be located. Given up: the specifically Soviet agitprop-newsreel flavour, and the phrase's later life as a proverb, which only the note can carry.

value.finding: It is the first line (and title) of Afanasy Fet's 1842 lyric, set to music the same year by A. E. Varlamov as the first-ever Fet romance; by 1850 Apollon Grigoriev called it 'almost a folk song', it appeared in songbooks from the 1850s on and stayed in the repertoire (Lemeshev, Pogudin), so any Russian reader in 1928 or 2013 heard it as a sung tune, not a book poem. In chapter XIV Ostap arrives at 5 a.m. with the widow Gritsatsuyeva's chair and explains, in guillemets, 'Вдовица спит и видит сон. Жаль было будить. «На заре ты ее не буди»' before quoting the note he left signed 'Твой Суслик' — the sentimental parlour romance serves as a mock-tender alibi for sneaking out of the bridal bed with the loot. John Richardson's English (lib.ru) renders it "'Don't wake her at dawn!'", and the romance is catalogued in English as 'Do not wake her at dawn' (ruverses, musopus). A Japanese song-title index glosses it 明け方に　君は彼女を目覚めさせるな and a singing translation by 小野光子 is titled 「あかつきに」; no printed Chinese title for the poem or for this passage of 十二把椅子 was found in search.

value.finding: Fyodor Ivanovich Vostrikov is the priest of the Church of Frol and Lavr in the provincial town N, who hears Madame Petukhova's deathbed confession and becomes the third, solo treasure-hunter; a seminarian who dodged the 1915 draft by taking orders, he is drawn as a petty entrepreneur (rabbits, 'marble' soap, the dreamed-of candle factory), and his letters to his wife parody Dostoevsky; the hunt ends with him mad in the Daryal Gorge. The three address forms are tonally distinct in the text: the narrator calls him 'духовная особа' (chapter XI, 'спросила духовная особа как можно язвительнее'), a mock-solemn officialese label; Vorobyaninov, kicking him over a chair, spits 'святой отец' as pure sarcasm and later sneers 'А святой отец?' inwardly (ch. XII); Bender greets him 'Здравствуйте, батюшка' 'с невыразимой сладостью', the folksy-affectionate form turned into honeyed mockery, before 'многоуважаемый служитель культа' and 'Почем опиум для народа?'. For a Russian reader the name belongs to a national comic canon (Pugovkin in Gaidai's 1971 film; a statue in Kharkov, 2001) and 'опиум для народа' is a proverb. Established renderings: English Richardson (lib.ru) 'Father Theodore Vostrikov', 'Holy Father', 'the cleric'; Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'Father Fyodor Vostrikov'; Chinese (Zhang Peiwen, PLPH 2004, Baidu) '神父费多尔' / '费奥多尔神父'; Japanese (Egawa Takashi, Shueisha 1966) 'フョードル神父', with ヴォストリコフ/ボストリコフ both attested.

value.finding: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov is the co-protagonist of The Twelve Chairs: a 52-year-old (born 1875) former uyezd marshal of the nobility of Stargorod who after 1917 is reduced to a registrar at the ZAGS (civil-registry office) desk for marriages and deaths in the town of N, and who hunts his mother-in-law's jewels with Ostap Bender. His childhood nickname Kisa ('kitty') is what Bender mostly calls him, alongside mock-titles like 'fieldmarshal' and 'district marshal of the Comanches'; the full name-and-patronymic is the narrator's and the pre-revolutionary world's formal address. For Russian readers around 2013 the name is instantly Sergei Filippov's gaunt, pince-nez Kisa from Gaidai's 1971 film (put on a Russian postal envelope in 2012; statues in Pyatigorsk 2008 and Kharkiv) and a byword for a fallen gentleman clinging to dignity, with lines like 'Gentlemen, I have not eaten for six days' in common use. English editions (Richardson 1971, Fisher 2011, Northwestern) and Wikipedia all use 'Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov'. Chinese editions split: Zhang Peiwen (PLPH 2004) and Xu Changhan (Houlang 2022) print 沃洛比亚尼诺夫, and Bai Huaxiong's Shanghai Translation 2022 edition is described with 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇; 沃罗比亚尼诺夫 is the newspaper-table form. value.finding: Verified against the Russian text (Wikisource, ch. II): the coffin-maker Bezenchuk says «господин Воробьянинов» three times — «Так как же прикажете, господин Воробьянинов?», «Не извольте беспокоиться, господин Воробьянинов», «А с гробом как, господин Воробьянинов?» — and wraps it in the old servile formulas «прикажете» / «не извольте беспокоиться». «Господин» was the pre-1917 title for a gentleman; from 1918 «товарищ» replaced it officially and «господин» came to mark either old-regime loyalty or ideological hostility, while «гражданин» was the neutral-official third term (Gramota.ru). In 1927 a tradesman still calling a former marshal of the nobility «господин» is thus a joke on both men as leftovers of the old world, set against the street «имени товарища Губернского» and the «товарищ» used by everyone else in the same pages. The novel is set in 1927 and published in 1928; the prompt's references to '2013', Durov and VKontakte are template residue and do not apply to this term. Established English coverage: Richardson's 1961 translation (lib.ru) renders it 'Mr. Vorobyaninov' and uses 'Comrade' for товарищ; I could not verify the wording of the Fisher (2011), Egawa (1969, ja) or Chinese translations for this line, so the zh/ja renderings below are reasoned choices, not confirmed quotations.

rendering.ja: ヴォロビャニノフの旦那（bind: господин → 旦那；товарищ → 同志；гражданин → 市民）

value.note_for_reader: The undertaker uses the pre-revolutionary 'gospodin' (gentleman/Mister), long replaced by 'comrade' — ten years after the Revolution, a sign that both men belong to the old world.
value.rationale: All three keep the connotation (a tradesman's old-regime deference to a former gentleman) and the fixed three-way contrast with Comrade/同志 and Citizen/公民/市民; 'Mister' spelled out keeps the denotation and only gains its markedness from that contrast, while 老爷 and 旦那 trade exact denotation ('Mr.') for the servile register that Bezenchuk's «не извольте беспокоиться» carries, so the joke lands without a note in zh/ja.

value.finding: Bezenchuk is the drunken, small-time coffin-maker of the town of N whose shabby shop opens the novel (Chapter I, «Безенчук и „нимфы“»); the text calls him 'гробовых дел мастер Безенчук' and, more plainly, 'мастер Безенчук', and pits him against the rival funeral firms «Нимфа» and the defunct «Милости просим». The formula 'X-ых дел мастер' is an old guild-style trade title (cf. 'золотых дел мастер' = goldsmith, 'часовых дел мастер' = watchmaker, marked 'устар.' in dictionaries), so applied to a hungover provincial coffin-knocker it is mock-solemn: the dignity of the title against the squalor of the trade. For a Russian reader the name is proverbial through the 1971 and 1976 films and his coffin-euphemism speech ('туды её в качель', 'что ни гроб, то огурчик'). English translators split: John Richardson (1961) flattens it to 'Bezenchuk, the undertaker'; Anne O. Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) keeps the craft with 'master coffin-maker Bezenchuk'. Chinese editions (张佩文, 人民文学 2004; 上海译文 2022; 徐昌翰, 江苏凤凰 2022) title the chapter 「别津丘克与'仙女'」 or 「别津丘克和'山林女神'」 and refer to him as 棺材匠 (the 2022 徐昌翰 text uses 寿材铺 for the shops); no Chinese source uses 掌柜. The Japanese translation is 江川卓's 『十二の椅子』 (集英社 1966 / 筑摩 1969), whose exact wording I could not fetch; Japanese web coverage of the character gives ベゼンチュク（棺職人）.
sources: https://jmedia.wiki/死を婉曲的に表現するロシア語のリスト/List_of_Russian-language_euphemisms_for_dying

rendering.ja: 棺桶職人ベゼンチュク

value.rationale: All three keep the denotation (he makes coffins, not merely arranges funerals) and the craftsman sense via 'master'/匠/職人, which lets the dry narration deliver the joke without a note; the guild-archaic flavour of 'дел мастер' is given up, and 掌柜 was rejected because it recasts him as a shop-owner in a Chinese idiom no existing edition uses. value.finding: Мельстрой was a real organisation, not an invention: the state technical office 'Мельстрой' (1921–22), then the State Joint-Stock Company 'Мельстрой' (1922–30) under VSNKh, later a state trust for building flour mills and grain elevators (Russian archive guides, RGAE fund 3896; the abbreviation dictionary glosses it 'Государственный трест по строительству мельниц и зерновых элеваторов'). The name is a standard NEP-era stump compound, мель(ничное) + строй(тельство). In the novel it occurs three times, all in Stargorod chapters IX, XII and XIII (Wikisource text): 'Потрясая город, проехал грузовик Мельстроя', 'у перегруженного грузовика Мельстроя лопнула рессора' (Polesov giving advice), and 'Грузовики Старкомхоза и Мельстроя развозили детей' — background props of Soviet provincial bustle, and to a 1928 reader an everyday brand name with the faintly comic sound of all such acronyms. Richardson's 1961 English (lib.ru text) expands it every time to 'the grain-mill-and-lift-construction administration', which is heavier than the original; I could not verify Fisher's 2011 rendering or any published Chinese or Japanese rendering (Google Books rate-limited, no snippet found).

rendering.ja: メリストロイ（製粉所建設トラスト）

value.note_for_reader: Melstroy: a real Soviet state company (1921–30) that built flour mills and grain elevators; the name is a typical Soviet stump-compound, mel'nitsa 'mill' + stroitel'stvo 'construction'.
value.rationale: Keeps the denotation (a mill-building state trust) and the acronym sound that marks it as a Soviet institution — transliterate 'Melstroy' with a two-word gloss on first appearance only, then bare 'Melstroy' ('a Melstroy truck'); gives up Richardson's full expansion, which kills the throwaway rhythm of 'Потрясая город, проехал грузовик Мельстроя'. In zh, 面粉厂 rather than 磨坊 because Melstroy built industrial flour mills, not village mills; ja follows the established ゴスプラン-style pattern of katakana plus a bracketed gloss.

value.finding: Мельстрой was a real organisation, not an invention: the state technical office 'Мельстрой' (1921–22), then the State Joint-Stock Company 'Мельстрой' (1922–30) under VSNKh, later a state trust for building flour mills and grain elevators (Russian archive guides, RGAE fund 3896; the abbreviation dictionary glosses it 'Государственный трест по строительству мельниц и зерновых элеваторов'). The name is a standard NEP-era stump compound, мель(ничное) + строй(тельство). In the novel it occurs three times, all in Stargorod chapters IX, XII and XIII (Wikisource text): 'Потрясая город, проехал грузовик Мельстроя', 'у перегруженного грузовика Мельстроя лопнула рессора' (Polesov giving advice), and 'Грузовики Старкомхоза и Мельстроя развозили детей' — background props of Soviet provincial bustle, and to a 1928 reader an everyday brand name with the faintly comic sound of all such acronyms. Richardson's 1961 English (lib.ru text) expands it every time to 'the grain-mill-and-lift-construction administration', which is heavier than the original; I could not verify Fisher's 2011 rendering or any published Chinese or Japanese rendering (Google Books rate-limited, no snippet found).

value.finding: In the novel the phrase is bureaucratic category language: the archivist Korobeinikov reads from the 1919 housing-department ledger that one walnut chair went 'товарищу Грицацуеву, как инвалиду империалистической войны, по его заявлению и резолюции завжилотделом т. Буркина' (ch. XI), and Ostap then repeats it mockingly in ch. XII. 'Империалистическая война' was the official Leninist-Soviet name for World War I (1914-18), used in Soviet encyclopedias and 1920s memory politics to brand the war as an unjust, predatory war between capitalist powers; the pre-revolutionary names 'Великая война' / 'Вторая Отечественная' were suppressed. 'Инвалид империалистической войны' was accordingly the welfare category of a man disabled in the tsarist army, as distinct from the privileged 'инвалид Красной Армии / гражданской войны'; the 1926 census recorded exactly these classes, and such men were treated with limited sympathy as 'victims of the criminal ambitions of tsarism' but ranked below Red Army invalids for pensions and priority. For a 1928 reader (and still for a Russian reader in 2013, who recognises the old officialese as a period marker) the label signals a small entitlement claim couched in Party jargon, which is why a chair ends up with Gritsatsuev. The 1961 Richardson English translation renders it 'imperialist war invalid'; the standard Chinese translation (张佩文, 人民文学 名著名译) has '帝国主义战争的残废军人'; no Japanese text (江川卓 訳, 筑摩書房) was accessible online, so the Japanese rendering follows the established term 傷痍軍人 for a disabled veteran.

value.finding: 'Империалистическая война' was the official early-Soviet name for World War I (1914–18), taken from Lenin's 1915 characterisation of the war as an imperialist one; Russian Wiktionary lists it as a historical Sovietism. 'Инвалид империалистической войны' was the corresponding welfare category: a man disabled in the tsarist army, entitled to a pension and to housing-department favours, but ranked in the 1920s social-security hierarchy below 'инвалиды Красной Армии' (Civil War veterans) and treated as a victim of tsarism rather than a hero. In the novel it appears in chapter XI as pure paperwork: the archivist reads out that one chair went 'товарищу Грицацуеву, как инвалиду империалистической войны, по его заявлению и резолюции завжилотделом'; Ostap then mockingly repeats the full formula. The comedy is the deadpan officialese, and the reader also knows the 'invalid' is dead and the chair is with his fat widow. Richardson's 1961 English translation renders it 'imperialist war invalid' both times; no Chinese or Japanese translation text was reachable, but 帝国主义战争 and 帝国主義戦争 are the established Marxist-lexicon terms in both languages.

value.finding: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov is the co-protagonist of The Twelve Chairs: a 52-year-old (born 1875) former uyezd marshal of the nobility of Stargorod who after 1917 is reduced to a registrar at the ZAGS (civil-registry office) desk for marriages and deaths in the town of N, and who hunts his mother-in-law's jewels with Ostap Bender. His childhood nickname Kisa ('kitty') is what Bender mostly calls him, alongside mock-titles like 'fieldmarshal' and 'district marshal of the Comanches'; the full name-and-patronymic is the narrator's and the pre-revolutionary world's formal address. For Russian readers around 2013 the name is instantly Sergei Filippov's gaunt, pince-nez Kisa from Gaidai's 1971 film (put on a Russian postal envelope in 2012; statues in Pyatigorsk 2008 and Kharkiv) and a byword for a fallen gentleman clinging to dignity, with lines like 'Gentlemen, I have not eaten for six days' in common use. English editions (Richardson 1971, Fisher 2011, Northwestern) and Wikipedia all use 'Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov'. Chinese editions split: Zhang Peiwen (PLPH 2004) and Xu Changhan (Houlang 2022) print 沃洛比亚尼诺夫, and Bai Huaxiong's Shanghai Translation 2022 edition is described with 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇; 沃罗比亚尼诺夫 is the newspaper-table form. Japanese coverage is unsettled (ヴォロビャニノフ in Russia Beyond JP, ヴォロビヤニノフ and ボロビヤニノフ in reviews); Egawa Taku's 1961/1969 translation could not be checked directly.

rendering.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃洛比亚尼诺夫
rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビャニノフ

value.note_for_reader: Name-and-patronymic (Ippolit Matveyevich) is the polite Russian address; Bender's 'Kisa' (kitty), 'chief' and 'marshal' are his own mocking epithets for the same man.
value.rationale: All three keep the full three-part name so the patronymic's formality and the gap to Bender's nicknames survive; the English form is the established one across both published translations, Chinese follows the two printed editions (沃洛) over the newspaper table (沃罗), Japanese follows the fuller ヴォ/ヴェ spelling used by Russia Beyond JP. Given up: the comic sparrow (воробей) echo in the surname and the reader's film-memory of Filippov, which no transliteration carries.

value.finding: The novel's co-protagonist: born 1875, a former uyezd (district) marshal of the nobility who after 1917 is a clerk at the ZAGS registry office in the town of N, recording deaths and marriages; 52 years old, tall, grey, with a groomed moustache. The narrators address him by name-and-patronymic throughout, which signals both his pre-revolutionary standing and the mock-solemn register; Bender alone uses the childhood nickname Киса ('Kitty') and mocking titles such as предводитель, фельдмаршал and 'уездный предводитель команчей'. For a Russian reader around 2013 he is a proverbial figure, a proud but helpless ex-aristocrat, fixed by the Gaidai (1971) and Zakharov (1976) films and by monuments in Pyatigorsk and Kharkiv. Established renderings: English editions and Wikidata use 'Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov' (Fisher's 2011 translation prints 'Matveevich', a spelling variant); the 1966/1969 Japanese translation by 江川卓 (Shueisha) transliterates the surname ヴォロビャニノフ (older blog citation: イポリット・マトベイッチ・ボロビヤニノフ), and current Japanese coverage uses イッポリート／キーサ・ヴォロビャニノフ; Chinese editions vary, 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺) gives 伊坡利·沃洛比亚尼诺夫 and the 2022 上海译文 edition (白桦熊) gives 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇, so 沃洛比亚尼诺夫/沃罗比亚尼诺夫 both circulate.

rendering.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビャニノフ

value.note_for_reader: Russians address adults formally by given name plus patronymic (father's name + -ovich/-evich); 'Ippolit Matveyevich' is respectful, and Bender's 'Kisa' ('Kitty') is a deliberately deflating childhood nickname.
value.rationale: Full transliteration with the patronymic keeps the denotation and the formal, faintly antiquated register that name-and-patronymic carries; the class flavour of a Russian patronymic is not native to any target language and is supplied by a single note rather than by the name. Bender's epithets (Kisa, предводитель, патрон, фельдмаршал) are bound separately and are not folded into this rendering.

value.finding: ДОПР = дом (общественно-)принудительных работ, the name given to ordinary prisons after a 1920 justice-commissariat decree renamed them 'houses of forced labour'; in the RSFSR the label faded after the 1922 code, but in the Ukrainian SSR (Ukr. БУПР) it stayed the everyday word for a prison through the 1920s (Kharkiv, Kyiv, Odessa, Zhytomyr ДОПРы are documented into 1929), which is why the two Odessans use it. It denotes a real prison with a work regime, not a workhouse or a camp. In the novel it occurs in Ch. VIII, Ostap to Pasha Emilievich: «Один мой знакомый тоже продавал государственную мебель. Теперь он пошел в монахи — сидит в допре», a joke on 'withdrawing from the world' = being locked up; and in the Ch. XXVII title «Замечательная допровская корзинка», Kislyarsky's ever-ready bed-table-cupboard for arrest, which lives on in modern Russian as a phrase for a packed 'in case they come for me' bag. A 2013 Russian reader knows допр only through this novel: it reads as a period-flavoured, faintly comic Soviet acronym for 'jail'. Richardson's English (lib.ru) already settles the tone: 'He now lives a monastic life in the penitentiary' and 'The Marvellous Prison Basket'; no published Chinese or Japanese rendering of the term was found online.

value.finding: ДОПР = дом (общественно-)принудительных работ, 'house of forced labour': a Soviet penal institution of the 1920s, especially in the Ukrainian SSR (Ukr. Commentaries to the novel gloss it as one variety of Soviet prison of the period, for sentences of roughly six months to two years for the 'not socially dangerous'. By 1928 it was a lower-case common noun in the Odessa/Ukraine speech Ilf and Petrov grew up with, meaning simply 'the clink'. In ch. VIII Ostap warns Pasha Emilevich: 'Один мой знакомый тоже продавал государственную мебель. Теперь он пошел в монахи — сидит в допре'; the joke is the substitution of 'taking monastic vows' (withdrawal from the world) for 'doing time', capped by the deflating slang word. The passage is absent from Richardson's 1961 English text (abridged), and I could not verify Fisher's 2011 rendering or the Chinese/Japanese editions online, so no established target rendering was found.

value.finding: A Soviet institution, not decor: from the early 1920s every factory, office, barracks, ship, dormitory and (as in ch. VIII, the 2nd House of Sobes) welfare home had a 'red corner' — a room or partitioned nook with a Lenin portrait or bust, red cloth, slogans, wall newspaper and a table of newspapers and pamphlets, used for literacy classes, collective newspaper readings, agitation and party/Komsomol meetings; Ushakov (1935) defines it as 'помещение для политической и культурно-просветительной работы'. The name puns on the peasant 'красный угол', the icon corner, so Lenin replaces the icons; after 1924 many were renamed 'ленинский уголок', and by the 1960s 'ленинская комната'. For a 1928 reader it was standard, slightly tedious officialese, and Ilf and Petrov's joke is that the pious room's only asset is a pre-revolutionary 'English chair' that Pasha Emilievich sells to a junk dealer while Ostap 'inspects it for fire safety'. Existing renderings: Richardson (1961) flattens it to 'recreation room' (kills the joke); English scholarship and journalism use 'Red Corner' (MSU glossary, The Russian Reader); Chinese coverage uses 红角/列宁角 (Zhihu on Rodchenko's workers' club); I found no established Japanese term, and could not verify Fisher's (2011) or the Chinese/Japanese book translations. (The prompt's line about 2013/Durov/VKontakte does not apply to this term.)

value.finding: A красный уголок was the room (or corner of a room) set aside in every Soviet workplace, barracks, dormitory or institution for agitation and political education: newspaper readings, literacy classes in the early 1920s, meetings, later party/Komsomol ceremonies, always with a Lenin bust or portrait, a wall newspaper and posters. It arose in Red Army barracks around 1921 and the name deliberately echoes the pre-revolutionary красный угол, the icon corner of a peasant house ('красный' there meaning 'beautiful/honoured'), so for a 1928 reader it was the secular altar of the new order, an official term used without irony. By the 1960s most were renamed 'Lenin rooms' and they faded into a dead ritual. In Chapter VIII the term is used deadpan: the Starsobes old-women's home has no primuses in its red corner, but it does have an English chair there. Richardson (1961) flattens it to 'recreation room'; scholarly and popular English coverage uses 'red corner'; Chinese coverage uses 红角 (alongside 列宁角); a Japanese Russian dictionary glosses it only descriptively as '(革命教育を行う)講習部屋', so no fixed Japanese term was found. Fisher's 2011 rendering could not be checked online.

value.finding: In Chapter XII («Знойная женщина — мечта поэта»), inside Ostap's inset «Рассказ о гусаре-схимнике», the hussar Count Aleksei Bulanov, now the hermit Evpl, finds his oak coffin infested with bedbugs and escalates through remedies: kerosene, then «порошок „Арагац“ против клопов» fetched from town («Но и „Арагац“ не помог»), then burning them with a splinter, and finally the private firm бр. Глик's pink liquid «Клопин» smelling of poisoned peach — all fail, and the ascetic ends up spending his days killing bugs. Арагац is the name of the highest mountain of Soviet Armenia, so the joke for a 1928 reader is a lofty, exotic brand name of NEP-era small-trade advertising slapped on a humble bedbug dust, in a passage Shcheglov's commentary reads as a parody of hagiographic demon-torment (Anatole France's Thaïs, Tolstoy's Father Sergius); Shcheglov does not gloss «Арагац» as an attested product, and web search turned up no advertisement or catalogue confirming a real 1920s powder of that name, so it may be invented on the pattern of real ones. Richardson's 1961 English translation omits the whole hermit story, so there is no established English rendering; Fisher's 2011 English, the Chinese (白桦熊, QQ Reading edition) and Japanese (江川卓) versions of this sentence could not be retrieved online. Standard geographic transliterations are Aragats (en), 阿拉加茨 (zh, as in 阿拉加茨山), アラガツ (ja, as in アラガツ山).

value.rationale: Keeps the denotation (a named commercial bedbug dust) and the mock-solemn register of a brand in quotation marks, using each language's standard transliteration of the mountain so the bare brand can recur in the escalation («Но и „Арагац“ не помог»); gives up the instant recognition of the Armenian mountain, which the one-line note restores.

value.finding: In Chapter XII («Знойная женщина — мечта поэта»), inside Ostap's inset «Рассказ о гусаре-схимнике», the hussar Count Aleksei Bulanov, now the hermit Evpl, finds his oak coffin infested with bedbugs and escalates through remedies: kerosene, then «порошок „Арагац“ против клопов» fetched from town («Но и „Арагац“ не помог»), then burning them with a splinter, and finally the private firm бр. Глик's pink liquid «Клопин» smelling of poisoned peach — all fail, and the ascetic ends up spending his days killing bugs. Арагац is the name of the highest mountain of Soviet Armenia, so the joke for a 1928 reader is a lofty, exotic brand name of NEP-era small-trade advertising slapped on a humble bedbug dust, in a passage Shcheglov's commentary reads as a parody of hagiographic demon-torment (Anatole France's Thaïs, Tolstoy's Father Sergius); Shcheglov does not gloss «Арагац» as an attested product, and web search turned up no advertisement or catalogue confirming a real 1920s powder of that name, so it may be invented on the pattern of real ones. Richardson's 1961 English translation omits the whole hermit story, so there is no established English rendering; Fisher's 2011 English, the Chinese (白桦熊, QQ Reading edition) and Japanese (江川卓) versions of this sentence could not be retrieved online. Standard geographic transliterations are Aragats (en), 阿拉加茨 (zh, as in 阿拉加茨山), アラガツ (ja, as in アラガツ山).

data.chapter_title: Глава IX. Где ваши локоны? (Chapter 9. Where Are Your Curls?)

sentences.ru: Остап омрачился.
sentences.en: Ostap's face darkened.
sentences.zh: 奥斯塔普的脸色阴沉下来。
sentences.ja: オスタップの顔が曇った。

sentences.ru: — Кислое дело, — сказал он, — пещера Лейхтвейса.
sentences.en: "A sour business," he said. "A Leichtweiss cave, straight out of the penny dreadfuls."
sentences.zh: “这事儿不妙，”他说，“莱希特韦斯的山洞（廉价冒险小说里的强盗窝）。”
sentences.ja: 「しけた話だ」と彼は言った。「ライヒトヴァイスの洞窟（三文冒険小説の盗賊の隠れ家）だな」

sentences.ru: Таинственный соперник.
sentences.en: "A mysterious rival."
sentences.zh: “一个神秘的对手。”
sentences.ja: 「謎の競争相手だ」

sentences.ru: Его нужно опередить, а морду ему мы всегда успеем пощупать.
sentences.en: "We have to get ahead of him; there'll always be time to rearrange his face."
sentences.zh: “得抢在他前头；揍他一顿的机会总会有的。”
sentences.ja: 「先を越さねばならん。面をぶん殴るのはいつでもできる」

sentences.ru: Пока друзья закусывали в пивной «Стенька Разин» и Остап разузнавал, в каком доме находился раньше жилотдел и какое учреждение находится в нем теперь, день кончился.
sentences.en: While the friends had a bite in the Stenka Razin beer-hall and Ostap found out which building had once housed the Housing Department and what institution occupied it now, the day came to an end.
sentences.zh: 两位朋友在“斯坚卡·拉辛”啤酒馆里吃着小菜，奥斯塔普打听着住房处从前设在哪座房子里、如今那里又是什么机关，这一天就这样过去了。
sentences.ja: 二人の友が「ステンカ・ラージン」ビアホールで軽く腹ごしらえをし、オスタップが住宅課がかつてどの建物にあったか、いまそこにどんな役所が入っているかを聞き出しているうちに、日は暮れた。

sentences.ru: Золотые битюги снова стали коричневыми.
sentences.en: The golden dray-horses turned brown again.
sentences.zh: 金色的挽马又变回了棕色。
sentences.ja: 金色に輝いていた荷馬車馬は、また茶色に戻った。

sentences.ru: Брильянтовые капли холодели на лету и плюхались оземь.
sentences.en: Diamond drops went cold in mid-air and plopped onto the ground.
sentences.zh: 钻石般的水滴在半空中变凉，啪嗒啪嗒落到地上。
sentences.ja: ダイヤモンドのような雫は宙を落ちるうちに冷え、ぴしゃりと地面に叩きつけられた。

sentences.ru: В пивных и ресторане «Феникс» пиво поднялось в цене: наступил вечер.
sentences.en: In the beer-halls and the Phoenix restaurant the price of beer went up: evening had come.
sentences.zh: 各家啤酒馆和“凤凰”饭店里的啤酒涨了价：夜晚来临了。
sentences.ja: ビアホールやレストラン「フェニックス」ではビールの値段が上がった。夜になったのだ。

sentences.ru: На Большой Пушкинской зажглись электрические лампы, и, возвращаясь домой с первой весенней прогулки, с барабанным топаньем прошел отряд пионеров.
sentences.en: On Bolshaya Pushkinskaya the electric lamps came on, and a troop of Young Pioneers, returning home from the first outing of spring, marched past with a drum-like tramp of feet.
sentences.zh: 大普希金街上亮起了电灯，一队少先队员从春天的第一次郊游归来，迈着鼓点般的步子走了过去。
sentences.ja: ボリシャヤ・プーシキン通りに電灯がともり、春最初の遠足から帰るピオネール（少年団）の一隊が、太鼓のような足音を響かせて通り過ぎた。

sentences.ru: Тигры, победы и кобры губплана таинственно светились под входящей в город луной.
sentences.en: The tigers, Victories and cobras of the Provincial Planning Board (Gubplan) glowed mysteriously beneath the moon as it entered the town.
sentences.zh: 省计划委员会大楼上的老虎、胜利女神和眼镜蛇，在进入城中的月亮下神秘地闪着光。
sentences.ja: 県計画委員会の虎と勝利の女神とコブラが、町に入ってくる月の下で神秘的に光っていた。

sentences.ru: Идя домой с замолчавшим вдруг Остапом, Ипполит Матвеевич посмотрел на губплановских тигров и кобр.
sentences.en: Walking home with Ostap, who had suddenly fallen silent, Ippolit Matveyevich looked at the Gubplan tigers and cobras.
sentences.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇同忽然沉默下来的奥斯塔普一道往家走，望了望省计划委员会的老虎和眼镜蛇。
sentences.ja: 急に黙り込んだオスタップと連れ立って家路をたどりながら、イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチは県計画委員会の虎とコブラを眺めた。

sentences.ru: В его время здесь помещалась губернская земская управа, и граждане очень гордились кобрами, считая их старгородской достопримечательностью.
sentences.en: In his day the building had housed the provincial zemstvo board (the old elected local council), and the citizens had been very proud of the cobras, regarding them as one of the sights of Stargorod.
sentences.zh: 在他那个年代，这里是省地方自治局的所在，市民们对那些眼镜蛇十分自豪，把它们当作斯塔尔戈罗德的一处名胜。
sentences.ja: 彼の時代、ここには県ゼムストヴォ（地方自治）庁が置かれており、市民たちはコブラをスタルゴロドの名物と考えて大いに誇りにしていたものだ。

sentences.ru: «Найду», — подумал Ипполит Матвеевич, вглядываясь в гипсовую победу.
sentences.en: "I'll find it," thought Ippolit Matveyevich, peering at the plaster Victory.
sentences.zh: “我会找到的。”伊波利特·马特维耶维奇想道，凝视着那尊石膏胜利女神。
sentences.ja: 「見つけてみせる」とイッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチは、石膏の勝利の女神をじっと見つめながら思った。

sentences.ru: Тигры ласково размахивали хвостами, кобры радостно сокращались, и душа Ипполита Матвеевича наполнилась уверенностью.
sentences.en: The tigers waved their tails affectionately, the cobras contracted joyfully, and the soul of Ippolit Matveyevich filled with confidence.
sentences.zh: 老虎亲昵地摇着尾巴，眼镜蛇欢快地蜷缩着身子，伊波利特·马特维耶维奇的心里充满了信心。
sentences.ja: 虎たちは親しげに尻尾を振り、コブラたちは嬉しそうに身をくねらせ、イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチの心は確信で満たされた。

sentences.ru: Категория:Двенадцать стульев (Ильф и Петров)
sentences.en: Category: The Twelve Chairs (Ilf and Petrov)
sentences.zh: 分类：十二把椅子（伊里夫与彼得罗夫）
sentences.ja: カテゴリ：十二の椅子（イリフとペトロフ）

translator_notes: The tigers, Victories and cobras are stucco sculptures on the facade of the Provincial Planning Board building (the former zemstvo board); a 'Victory' here is a winged statue of the goddess of victory, not a triumph.
Bolshaya Pushkinskaya is the pre-revolutionary name of Red Army Street; the narrator uses the old name here, as the townspeople still do.
The closing line 'Категория:…' is a Wikisource category tag carried over from the source page, not part of the novel's text.

data.chapter_title: Глава XII. Знойная женщина — мечта поэта (Chapter XII. A Sultry Woman, a Poet's Dream)

sentences.ru: Подвиг схимника Евпла наполнил удивлением обитель.
sentences.en: The feat of the schema-monk Yevpl filled the cloister with astonishment.
sentences.zh: 大苦修士叶夫普尔的苦行壮举让整座修道院惊叹不已。
sentences.ja: 大スヒマ修道士エフプルの苦行は、修道院じゅうを驚嘆で満たした。

sentences.ru: Он ел только сухари, запас которых ему возобновляли раз в три месяца.
sentences.en: He ate nothing but dried rusks, a stock of which was replenished for him once every three months.
sentences.zh: 他只吃干面包片，存货每三个月给他补充一次。
sentences.ja: 彼は乾パンしか口にせず、その蓄えは三か月に一度補充された。

sentences.ru: Так прошло двадцать лет.
sentences.en: Twenty years passed in this way.
sentences.zh: 二十年就这样过去了。
sentences.ja: こうして二十年が過ぎた。

sentences.ru: Евпл считал свою жизнь мудрой, правильной и единственно верной.
sentences.en: Yevpl considered his life wise, correct and the only true one.
sentences.zh: 叶夫普尔认为自己的生活是明智的、正确的、唯一正当的。
sentences.ja: エフプルは自分の生き方を賢明で、正しく、唯一まことのものだと考えていた。

sentences.ru: Жить ему стало необыкновенно легко, и мысли его были хрустальными.
sentences.en: Living had become extraordinarily easy for him, and his thoughts were crystalline.
sentences.zh: 他活得异常轻松，思想澄澈如水晶。
sentences.ja: 生きることは彼にとって驚くほど楽になり、その思考は水晶のように澄みきっていた。

sentences.ru: Он постиг жизнь и понял, что иначе жить нельзя.
sentences.en: He had fathomed life and understood that there was no other way to live.
sentences.zh: 他参透了人生，明白了人不可能有别的活法。
sentences.ja: 彼は人生を悟り、これ以外の生き方はありえないと理解した。

sentences.ru: Однажды он с удивлением заметил, что на том месте, где он в продолжение двадцати лет привык находить сухари, ничего не было.
sentences.en: One day he noticed with surprise that in the place where for twenty years he had been accustomed to find his rusks there was nothing at all.
sentences.zh: 有一天，他惊讶地发现，二十年来他一向能在那里找到干面包片的地方，什么也没有了。
sentences.ja: ある日、彼は驚きとともに気づいた。二十年間ずっと乾パンが置かれていたはずの場所に、何もないのである。

sentences.ru: Он не ел четыре дня.
sentences.en: He did not eat for four days.
sentences.zh: 他四天没有吃东西。
sentences.ja: 彼は四日間、何も食べなかった。

sentences.ru: На пятый день пришел неизвестный ему старик в лаптях и сказал, что монахов выселили большевики и устроили в обители совхоз.
sentences.en: On the fifth day an old man he did not know came in bast shoes and said that the Bolsheviks had turned the monks out and set up a state farm in the cloister.
sentences.zh: 第五天，来了一个他不认识的穿树皮鞋的老头，说布尔什维克把修士们赶走了，在修道院里办起了国营农场。
sentences.ja: 五日目に、見知らぬ樹皮靴（ラプチ）姿の老人がやって来て、修道士たちはボリシェヴィキに追い出され、修道院には国営農場（ソフホーズ）が作られたと告げた。

sentences.ru: Оставив немного сухарей, старик, плача, ушел.
sentences.en: Leaving a few rusks, the old man went away, weeping.
sentences.zh: 老头留下一点干面包片，哭着走了。
sentences.ja: 老人は乾パンを少し置いて、泣きながら去っていった。

sentences.ru: Схимник не понял старика.
sentences.en: The schema-monk did not understand the old man.
sentences.zh: 大苦修士没有听懂老头的话。
sentences.ja: 大スヒマ修道士には老人の言うことがわからなかった。

sentences.ru: Светлый и тихий, он лежал в гробу и радовался познанию жизни.
sentences.en: Serene and quiet, he lay in his coffin and rejoiced in his knowledge of life.
sentences.zh: 他安详而宁静地躺在棺材里，为自己参透了人生而欢喜。
sentences.ja: 澄みきって静かに、彼は棺の中に横たわり、人生を悟った喜びに浸っていた。

sentences.ru: Старик крестьянин продолжал носить сухари.
sentences.en: The old peasant went on bringing rusks.
sentences.zh: 老农夫继续给他送干面包片。
sentences.ja: 老いた百姓は、その後も乾パンを運びつづけた。

sentences.ru: Так прошло еще несколько никем не потревоженных лет.
sentences.en: Several more years passed in this way, disturbed by no one.
sentences.zh: 又这样过了几年，没有任何人来打扰。
sentences.ja: こうして、誰にも邪魔されぬ歳月がさらに何年か過ぎた。

sentences.ru: Однажды только дверь землянки растворилась, и несколько человек, согнувшись, вошли в нее.
sentences.en: Only once did the door of the dugout swing open, and several men, stooping, came in.
sentences.zh: 只有一次，地窖的门打开了，几个人弯着腰走了进来。
sentences.ja: ただ一度だけ、土小屋の扉が開いて、数人の男が身をかがめて入ってきたことがあった。

sentences.ru: Они подошли к гробу и принялись молча рассматривать старца.
sentences.en: They came up to the coffin and began silently examining the elder.
sentences.zh: 他们走到棺材跟前，默默地打量起这位长老来。
sentences.ja: 彼らは棺に歩み寄り、黙って長老を眺めはじめた。

sentences.ru: Это были рослые люди в сапогах со шпорами, в огромных галифе и с маузерами в деревянных полированных ящиках.
sentences.en: They were tall men in spurred boots and vast riding breeches, with Mausers in polished wooden holsters.
sentences.zh: 那是几个穿马靴带马刺、宽大马裤、腰挎木匣毛瑟枪的高个子。
sentences.ja: 拍車付き長靴に幅広の乗馬ズボン、磨かれた木製ホルスターのモーゼル拳銃をさげた大男たちだった。

sentences.ru: Старец лежал в гробу, вытянув руки, и смотрел на пришельцев лучезарным взглядом.
sentences.en: The elder lay in the coffin with his arms stretched out and gazed at the visitors with a radiant look.
sentences.zh: 长老躺在棺材里，双手伸直，用光辉灿烂的目光望着这些来客。
sentences.ja: 長老は両腕を伸ばして棺の中に横たわり、光り輝くまなざしで来訪者たちを見つめていた。

sentences.ru: Длинная и легкая седая борода закрывала половину гроба.
sentences.en: A long, wispy grey beard covered half the coffin.
sentences.zh: 一把又长又轻软的白胡子遮住了半口棺材。
sentences.ja: 長く軽やかな白いあごひげが、棺の半分を覆っていた。

sentences.ru: Незнакомцы зазвенели шпорами, пожали плечами и удалились, бережно прикрыв за собою дверь.
sentences.en: The strangers jingled their spurs, shrugged their shoulders and withdrew, carefully closing the door behind them.
sentences.zh: 陌生人们马刺一响，耸了耸肩，便退了出去，小心地把门带上。
sentences.ja: 見知らぬ男たちは拍車を鳴らし、肩をすくめて、後ろ手にそっと扉を閉めて立ち去った。

sentences.ru: Время шло.
sentences.en: Time went on.
sentences.zh: 时光流逝。
sentences.ja: 時は流れた。

sentences.ru: Жизнь раскрылась перед схимником во всей своей полноте и сладости.
sentences.en: Life unfolded before the schema-monk in all its fullness and sweetness.
sentences.zh: 人生在大苦修士面前展现出它全部的丰盈与甘美。
sentences.ja: 人生はその充溢と甘美のすべてをもって、大スヒマ修道士の前に開けていた。

sentences.ru: В ночь, наступившую за тем днем, когда схимник окончательно понял, что все в его познании светло, он неожиданно проснулся.
sentences.en: On the night that followed the day when the schema-monk finally understood that everything in his knowledge was luminous, he unexpectedly woke up.
sentences.zh: 就在大苦修士彻底明白自己的悟性中一切皆已澄明的那一天，当夜他忽然醒了过来。
sentences.ja: 自分の悟りの中ではすべてが澄みわたっていると大スヒマ修道士がついに理解した、その日の夜のこと、彼は不意に目を覚ました。

sentences.ru: Это его удивило.
sentences.en: This surprised him.
sentences.zh: 这使他吃了一惊。
sentences.ja: これには彼も驚いた。

sentences.ru: Он никогда не просыпался ночью.
sentences.en: He never woke at night.
sentences.zh: 他从来不曾在夜里醒过。
sentences.ja: 夜中に目を覚ましたことなど、一度もなかったのだ。

sentences.ru: Размышляя о том, что его разбудило, он снова заснул и сейчас же опять проснулся, чувствуя сильное жжение в спине.
sentences.en: Pondering what had woken him, he fell asleep again and at once woke up once more, feeling a fierce burning in his back.
sentences.zh: 他一边琢磨是什么把自己弄醒的，一边又睡着了，可马上又醒了，觉得背上火辣辣地灼痛。
sentences.ja: 何に起こされたのかと考えているうちに、彼はまた眠りに落ち、そしてすぐにまた目を覚ました。背中に強い灼けるような痛みを感じたのだ。

sentences.ru: Постигая причину этого жжения, он старался заснуть, но не мог.
sentences.en: Trying to fathom the cause of this burning, he did his best to fall asleep, but could not.
sentences.zh: 他一面参究这灼痛的缘由，一面努力想睡着，却睡不着了。
sentences.ja: この灼熱の原因を悟ろうと努めながら、彼は眠ろうとしたが、眠れなかった。

sentences.ru: Что-то мешало ему.
sentences.en: Something was troubling him.
sentences.zh: 有什么东西在妨碍他。
sentences.ja: 何かが彼の邪魔をしていた。

sentences.ru: Он не спал до утра.
sentences.en: He did not sleep until morning.
sentences.zh: 他一直到早晨都没有睡着。
sentences.ja: 彼は朝まで眠れなかった。

sentences.ru: В следующую ночь его снова кто-то разбудил.
sentences.en: The next night someone woke him again.
sentences.zh: 第二天夜里，又有什么东西把他弄醒了。
sentences.ja: 次の夜も、また何者かが彼を起こした。

sentences.ru: Он проворочался до утра, тихо стеная и незаметно для самого себя почесывая руки.
sentences.en: He tossed and turned until morning, moaning softly and, without noticing it himself, scratching his arms.
sentences.zh: 他翻来覆去直到天亮，轻声呻吟着，不知不觉地挠着胳膊。
sentences.ja: 彼は朝まで寝返りを打ちつづけ、低くうめきながら、自分でも気づかぬうちに腕をかきむしっていた。

sentences.ru: Днем, поднявшись, он случайно заглянул в гроб.
sentences.en: In the daytime, having got up, he happened to glance into the coffin.
sentences.zh: 白天起身之后，他无意中朝棺材里看了一眼。
sentences.ja: 昼間、起き上がったとき、彼は何気なく棺の中をのぞきこんだ。

sentences.ru: Тогда он понял все: по углам его мрачной постели быстро перебегали вишневые клопы.
sentences.en: Then he understood everything: in the corners of his gloomy bed, cherry-red bedbugs were scurrying to and fro.
sentences.zh: 这时他全明白了：在他那阴森的卧榻的角落里，樱桃红色的臭虫正在飞快地窜来窜去。
sentences.ja: そのとき彼はすべてを理解した。陰気な寝床の隅々を、桜桃色の南京虫がすばやく走り回っていたのである。

sentences.ru: Схимнику сделалось противно.
sentences.en: The schema-monk felt disgusted.
sentences.zh: 大苦修士感到恶心。
sentences.ja: 大スヒマ修道士は嫌悪をおぼえた。

sentences.ru: В этот же день пришел старик с сухарями.
sentences.en: That same day the old man came with the rusks.
sentences.zh: 就在这一天，老头送干面包片来了。
sentences.ja: その同じ日、老人が乾パンを持ってやって来た。

sentences.ru: И вот подвижник, молчавший двадцать пять лет, заговорил.
sentences.en: And then the ascetic, who had kept silent for twenty-five years, spoke.
sentences.zh: 于是，沉默了二十五年的苦行者开口说话了。
sentences.ja: そしてここに、二十五年間沈黙を守ってきた苦行者が口を開いた。

sentences.ru: Он попросил принести ему немножко керосину.
sentences.en: He asked to be brought a little kerosene.
sentences.zh: 他请老头给他带一点煤油来。
sentences.ja: 灯油を少し持ってきてほしい、と彼は頼んだのである。

sentences.ru: Услышав речь великого молчальника, крестьянин опешил.
sentences.en: Hearing the great silent one speak, the peasant was dumbfounded.
sentences.zh: 听见这位伟大的缄默者开口说话，农夫愣住了。
sentences.ja: 偉大なる沈黙者の言葉を聞いて、百姓は呆然とした。

sentences.ru: Однако, стыдясь и пряча бутылочку, он принес керосин.
sentences.en: Nevertheless, ashamed and hiding the little bottle, he brought the kerosene.
sentences.zh: 不过，他还是把煤油送来了，羞愧地把小瓶子藏在身上。
sentences.ja: それでも彼は、恥じ入りながら小瓶を隠し持って、灯油を運んできた。

sentences.ru: Как только старик ушел, отшельник дрожащей рукой смазал все швы и пазы гроба.
sentences.en: As soon as the old man had gone, the hermit with a trembling hand smeared every seam and groove of the coffin.
sentences.zh: 老头一走，隐修士就用颤抖的手把棺材的每一道缝隙和槽口都抹上了煤油。
sentences.ja: 老人が去るやいなや、隠者は震える手で棺の継ぎ目や溝という溝に灯油を塗りこんだ。

sentences.ru: Впервые за три дня Евпл заснул спокойно.
sentences.en: For the first time in three days Yevpl slept peacefully.
sentences.zh: 三天来，叶夫普尔头一次安稳地睡着了。
sentences.ja: 三日ぶりに、エフプルは安らかに眠った。

sentences.ru: Его ничто не потревожило.
sentences.en: Nothing disturbed him.
sentences.zh: 什么也没有打扰他。
sentences.ja: 何ものも彼を煩わせなかった。

sentences.ru: Смазывал он керосином гроб и в следующие дни.
sentences.en: He smeared the coffin with kerosene on the following days as well.
sentences.zh: 接下来的几天，他也照样往棺材上抹煤油。
sentences.ja: その後の日々も、彼は棺に灯油を塗りつづけた。

sentences.ru: Но через два месяца понял, что керосином вывести клопов нельзя.
sentences.en: But after two months he realised that kerosene could not get rid of bedbugs.
sentences.zh: 可是两个月以后他明白了，煤油是灭不了臭虫的。
sentences.ja: だが二か月後、灯油では南京虫を退治できないことを悟った。

sentences.ru: По ночам он быстро переворачивался и громко молился, но молитвы помогали еще меньше керосина.
sentences.en: At night he turned over rapidly and prayed aloud, but the prayers helped even less than the kerosene.
sentences.zh: 夜里他急速地翻着身，大声祈祷，可祈祷比煤油还不管用。
sentences.ja: 夜ごと彼はせわしなく寝返りを打ち、声高に祈ったが、祈りは灯油よりもさらに効き目がなかった。

sentences.ru: Прошло полгода в невыразимых мучениях, прежде чем отшельник обратился к старику снова.
sentences.en: Six months of inexpressible torment passed before the hermit turned to the old man again.
sentences.zh: 在难以言表的折磨中过了半年，隐修士才再次向老头求助。
sentences.ja: 言葉に尽くせぬ苦しみのうちに半年が過ぎて、隠者はようやくふたたび老人に頼んだ。

sentences.ru: Вторая просьба еще больше поразила старика.
sentences.en: The second request astounded the old man even more.
sentences.zh: 第二个请求更加让老头大吃一惊。
sentences.ja: 二度目の頼みは、老人をさらに驚かせた。

sentences.ru: Схимник просил привезти ему из города порошок «Арагац» против клопов.
sentences.en: The schema-monk asked him to bring 'Aragats' bedbug powder from town.
sentences.zh: 大苦修士请他从城里捎来“阿拉加茨”灭臭虫粉。
sentences.ja: 大スヒマ修道士は、町から南京虫駆除粉「アラガツ」を買ってきてほしいと頼んだのである。

sentences.ru: Но и «Арагац» не помог.
sentences.en: But 'Aragats' bedbug powder did not help either.
sentences.zh: 可是“阿拉加茨”灭臭虫粉也没有用。
sentences.ja: だが南京虫駆除粉「アラガツ」も効かなかった。

sentences.ru: Клопы размножались необыкновенно быстро.
sentences.en: The bedbugs multiplied with extraordinary speed.
sentences.zh: 臭虫繁殖得异常迅速。
sentences.ja: 南京虫は驚くべき速さで殖えていった。

sentences.ru: Могучее здоровье схимника, которого не могло сломить двадцатипятилетнее постничество, заметно ухудшалось.
sentences.en: The schema-monk's mighty constitution, which twenty-five years of fasting had been unable to break, was visibly deteriorating.
sentences.zh: 大苦修士那二十五年斋戒都未能摧垮的强健体魄，明显地衰弱下去了。
sentences.ja: 二十五年の断食にも屈しなかった大スヒマ修道士の頑健な体は、目に見えて衰えていった。

sentences.ru: Началась темная, отчаянная жизнь.
sentences.en: A dark, desperate life began.
sentences.zh: 黑暗而绝望的生活开始了。
sentences.ja: 暗い、絶望的な生活が始まった。

sentences.ru: Гроб стал казаться схимнику Евплу омерзительным и неудобным.
sentences.en: The coffin began to seem to the schema-monk Yevpl loathsome and uncomfortable.
sentences.zh: 在大苦修士叶夫普尔看来，棺材变得又可憎又不舒服了。
sentences.ja: 大スヒマ修道士エフプルには、棺がおぞましく、寝心地の悪いものに思われてきた。

sentences.ru: Ночью, по совету крестьянина, он жег клопов лучиной.
sentences.en: At night, on the peasant's advice, he burned the bedbugs with a splinter of kindling.
sentences.zh: 夜里，他按农夫的主意，用点着的松明烧臭虫。
sentences.ja: 夜には、百姓の勧めにしたがって、火をつけた松明（たいまつ）代わりの木片で南京虫を焼いた。

sentences.ru: Клопы умирали, но не сдавались.
sentences.en: The bedbugs died, but they did not surrender.
sentences.zh: 臭虫死了，可并不投降。
sentences.ja: 南京虫は死んでいったが、降参はしなかった。

translator_notes: The 'schema' (схима) is the strictest grade of Orthodox monastic vows; a schema-monk (схимник) withdraws almost entirely from the world, which is why Yevpl's twenty-five-year silence and coffin-bed are presented as a recognised, if extreme, form of piety.
The 'splinter' (лучина) in the penultimate sentence is a thin sliver of resinous wood that Russian peasants burned for light before kerosene lamps; here it doubles as a bedbug-burning tool.

data.chapter_title: Глава XIII. Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы! (Chapter XIII. Breathe Deeper: You're Excited!)

sentences.ru: — Ну, будем считать через десять.
sentences.en: "Well, let's call it ten.
sentences.zh: “好吧，就算十年。
sentences.ja: 「まあ、十年と見ておこう。

sentences.ru: Теперь — акционерное общество.
sentences.en: Now, the joint-stock company.
sentences.zh: 接下来——股份公司。
sentences.ja: 次に――株式会社だ。

sentences.ru: Кто войдет?
sentences.en: Who'll come in?
sentences.zh: 谁来入股？
sentences.ja: 誰が加わる？

sentences.ru: Пищетрест, Маслоцентр.
sentences.en: The Food Trust, the Dairy Cooperative Centre (Maslotsentr).
sentences.zh: 食品托拉斯，奶油合作社中心。
sentences.ja: 食品トラスト、バター協同組合中央会（マスロツェントル）。

sentences.ru: Канатчикам трамвай нужен?
sentences.en: Does the rope works need a tram?
sentences.zh: 缆绳厂需要电车吗？
sentences.ja: ロープ工場に路面電車は要るか？

sentences.ru: Нужен!
sentences.en: It does!
sentences.zh: 需要！
sentences.ja: 要る！

sentences.ru: Мы до вокзала грузовые вагоны отправлять будем.
sentences.en: We'll be running freight cars out to the railway station.
sentences.zh: 我们要开货运车厢直达火车站。
sentences.ja: 駅まで貨物車両を走らせるんだからな。

sentences.ru: Значит, канатчики!
sentences.en: So, the rope works!
sentences.zh: 所以，缆绳厂算一个！
sentences.ja: というわけで、ロープ工場だ！

sentences.ru: НКПС, может быть, даст немного.
sentences.en: The Commissariat of Transport (NKPS) may give a little.
sentences.zh: 交通人民委员部也许能给一点。
sentences.ja: 交通人民委員部も、いくらか出してくれるかもしれん。

sentences.ru: Ну, губисполком даст.
sentences.en: Well, the Provincial Executive Committee will give.
sentences.zh: 省执行委员会嘛，会给的。
sentences.ja: それから県執行委員会は出す。

sentences.ru: Это уж обязательно.
sentences.en: That's a certainty.
sentences.zh: 这是一定的。
sentences.ja: これはもう間違いない。

sentences.ru: А раз начнем — Госбанк и Комбанк дадут ссуду.
sentences.en: And once we've started, the State Bank and the Communal Bank will give us a loan.
sentences.zh: 只要一开工——国家银行和市政银行就会贷款。
sentences.ja: いったん始めれば――国立銀行と市営銀行が融資してくれる。

sentences.ru: Вот такой мой планчик.
sentences.en: That's my little plan.
sentences.zh: 这就是我的小计划。
sentences.ja: これが俺のちょっとした計画だ。

sentences.ru: В пятницу на президиуме губисполкома разговор будет.
sentences.en: On Friday it comes up before the presidium of the Provincial Executive Committee.
sentences.zh: 星期五省执行委员会主席团要讨论这件事。
sentences.ja: 金曜日に県執行委員会の幹部会でこの話が出る。

sentences.ru: Если решимся — за вами остановка.
sentences.en: If we decide to go ahead, it's up to you."
sentences.zh: 要是决定干——就看您的了。”
sentences.ja: やると決まったら――あとはあなた次第です。」

sentences.ru: Треухов до поздней ночи взволнованно стирал белье и объяснял жене преимущества трамвайного транспорта перед гужевым.
sentences.en: Until late that night Treukhov, in a state of excitement, washed the linen and explained to his wife the advantages of tram transport over horse-drawn.
sentences.zh: 特列乌霍夫激动地洗衣服洗到深夜，一边向妻子讲解电车运输比马车运输的种种优越性。
sentences.ja: トレウーホフは夜更けまで、興奮に駆られて洗濯をしながら、路面電車が馬車輸送にまさる点を妻に説いて聞かせた。

sentences.ru: В пятницу вопрос решился благоприятно.
sentences.en: On Friday the question was settled favourably.
sentences.zh: 星期五，问题得到了顺利解决。
sentences.ja: 金曜日、問題は好ましい方向に決着した。

sentences.ru: И начались муки.
sentences.en: And the torments began.
sentences.zh: 于是苦难开始了。
sentences.ja: そして苦難が始まった。

sentences.ru: Акционерное общество сколачивали с великой натугой.
sentences.en: The joint-stock company was knocked together with enormous strain.
sentences.zh: 股份公司是费了九牛二虎之力才拼凑起来的。
sentences.ja: 株式会社は、たいへんな力業でどうにか寄せ集められた。

sentences.ru: НКПС то вступал, то не вступал в число акционеров.
sentences.en: The Commissariat of Transport (NKPS) was one moment among the shareholders and the next moment not.
sentences.zh: 交通人民委员部一会儿加入股东行列，一会儿又退出。
sentences.ja: 交通人民委員部は株主に加わったかと思えば、また加わらなかった。

sentences.ru: Пищетрест всячески старался вместо 15 % акций получить только десять.
sentences.en: The Food Trust tried by every means to take only ten per cent of the shares instead of fifteen.
sentences.zh: 食品托拉斯千方百计想把百分之十五的股份减为百分之十。
sentences.ja: 食品トラストは株式の十五パーセントではなく十パーセントだけで済まそうと、あの手この手を使った。

sentences.ru: Наконец, весь пакет акций был распределен, хотя и не обошлось без столкновений.
sentences.en: At last the whole block of shares was allotted, though not without clashes.
sentences.zh: 最后，全部股份总算分配完毕，尽管其间少不了争执。
sentences.ja: ついに全株式が割り当てられたが、衝突なしには済まなかった。

sentences.ru: Гаврилина за нажим вызвали в ГубКК.
sentences.en: Gavrilin was summoned before the Provincial Party Control Commission for applying pressure.
sentences.zh: 加夫里林因为施压被叫到省党监察委员会去了。
sentences.ja: ガヴリーリンは圧力をかけたかどで県党統制委員会に呼び出された。

sentences.ru: Впрочем, все обошлось благополучно.
sentences.en: Still, it all passed off safely.
sentences.zh: 不过，一切都平安无事地过去了。
sentences.ja: もっとも、すべて無事に収まった。

sentences.ru: Оставалось начать.
sentences.en: It only remained to begin.
sentences.zh: 剩下的就是开工了。
sentences.ja: あとは始めるだけだった。

sentences.ru: — Ну, товарищ Треухов, — сказал Гаврилин, — начинай.
sentences.en: "Well, Comrade Treukhov," said Gavrilin, "get started.
sentences.zh: “好啦，特列乌霍夫同志，”加夫里林说，“开始吧。
sentences.ja: 「さあ、トレウーホフ同志」とガヴリーリンは言った。「始めろ。

sentences.ru: Чувствуешь, что можешь построить?
sentences.en: Feel you can build it?
sentences.zh: 你觉得自己能建成吗？
sentences.ja: 建てられる、という手応えはあるか？

sentences.ru: То-то.
sentences.en: That's the spirit.
sentences.zh: 这就对了。
sentences.ja: そうこなくちゃな。

sentences.ru: Это тебе не ешака купить.
sentences.en: This isn't like buying a donkey, you know."
sentences.zh: 这可不是买头毛驴那么简单。”
sentences.ja: ロバを一頭買うのとはわけが違うぞ。」

sentences.ru: Треухов утонул в работе.
sentences.en: Treukhov drowned in work.
sentences.zh: 特列乌霍夫一头扎进了工作。
sentences.ja: トレウーホフは仕事に没頭した。

sentences.ru: Пришла пора великого дела, о котором он мечтал долгие годы.
sentences.en: The time had come for the great undertaking he had dreamed of for so many years.
sentences.zh: 他多年梦寐以求的伟大事业的时刻到来了。
sentences.ja: 長年夢見てきた大事業の時が来たのだ。

sentences.ru: Писались сметы, составлялся план постройки, делали заказы.
sentences.en: Estimates were drawn up, a construction plan was compiled, orders were placed.
sentences.zh: 编制预算，制订施工计划，下达订单。
sentences.ja: 見積りが書かれ、建設計画が組まれ、注文が出された。

sentences.ru: Трудности возникали там, где их меньше всего ожидали.
sentences.en: Difficulties cropped up where they were least expected.
sentences.zh: 困难总是出现在最料想不到的地方。
sentences.ja: 困難は、いちばん予想していなかったところから持ち上がった。

sentences.ru: В городе не оказалось специалистов-бетонщиков, и их пришлось выписать из Ленинграда.
sentences.en: The town turned out to have no concrete specialists, and they had to be sent for from Leningrad.
sentences.zh: 城里找不到混凝土专业工人，只好从列宁格勒调来。
sentences.ja: 町にはコンクリート工の専門家がいないことがわかり、レニングラードから呼び寄せなければならなかった。

sentences.ru: Гаврилин торопил, но заводы обещались дать машины только через полтора года.
sentences.en: Gavrilin kept hurrying things along, but the factories promised the machinery only in a year and a half.
sentences.zh: 加夫里林一个劲儿地催，可工厂答应一年半以后才能交付机器。
sentences.ja: ガヴリーリンは急かしたが、工場は機械を一年半後にしか納められないと言ってきた。

sentences.ru: А нужны они были самое позднее через год.
sentences.en: And it was needed within a year at the very latest.
sentences.zh: 而机器最迟一年后就得用上。
sentences.ja: ところが機械は遅くとも一年後には必要だった。

sentences.ru: Подействовала только угроза заказать машины за границей.
sentences.en: Only the threat of ordering the machinery abroad had any effect.
sentences.zh: 只有以到国外订购机器相威胁才管了用。
sentences.ja: 効き目があったのは、機械を外国に発注するぞという脅しだけだった。

sentences.ru: Потом пошли неприятности помельче.
sentences.en: Then came the smaller troubles.
sentences.zh: 接着是些较小的麻烦。
sentences.ja: それから、こまごました面倒が続いた。

sentences.ru: То нельзя было найти фасонного железа нужных размеров, то вместо пропитанных шпал предлагали непропитанные.
sentences.en: Now there was no shaped iron to be found in the right sizes; now untreated sleepers were offered instead of creosoted ones.
sentences.zh: 一会儿找不到所需尺寸的型钢，一会儿又拿未经防腐浸渍的枕木来顶替浸渍过的。
sentences.ja: 必要な寸法の型鋼が見つからないかと思えば、防腐処理済みの枕木の代わりに未処理のものを寄こしてくる。

sentences.ru: Наконец, дали то, что нужно, но Треухов, поехавший сам на шпалопропиточный завод, забраковал 60 % шпал.
sentences.en: At last they delivered what was needed, but Treukhov, who went to the sleeper-treatment plant himself, rejected 60 % of the sleepers.
sentences.zh: 最后总算给了所需的东西，可特列乌霍夫亲自跑到枕木浸渍厂去，把百分之六十的枕木都判了不合格。
sentences.ja: ようやく必要なものが届いたが、みずから枕木防腐工場へ出向いたトレウーホフは、枕木の六十パーセントを不合格にした。

sentences.ru: В чугунных частях были раковины.
sentences.en: The cast-iron parts had blowholes.
sentences.zh: 铸铁件上有砂眼。
sentences.ja: 鋳鉄部品には鬆が入っていた。

sentences.ru: Лес был сырой.
sentences.en: The timber was green.
sentences.zh: 木料是湿的。
sentences.ja: 材木は乾いていなかった。

sentences.ru: Рельсы были хороши, но они стали прибывать с опозданием на месяц.
sentences.en: The rails were good, but they began arriving a month late.
sentences.zh: 钢轨倒是不错，可交货晚了一个月。
sentences.ja: レールは良品だったが、一か月遅れで届きはじめた。

sentences.ru: Гаврилин часто приезжал в старом простуженном «фиате» на постройку станции.
sentences.en: Gavrilin often drove out to the power-station site in an old, wheezing Fiat.
sentences.zh: 加夫里林常常坐着一辆老掉牙、像得了伤风似的“菲亚特”来到发电站工地。
sentences.ja: ガヴリーリンは、風邪でも引いたようにぜいぜい言う古い「フィアット」で、しばしば発電所の建設現場にやって来た。

sentences.ru: Здесь между ним и Треуховым вспыхивали перебранки.
sentences.en: There, squabbles would flare up between him and Treukhov.
sentences.zh: 在那里，他和特列乌霍夫之间常常爆发口角。
sentences.ja: そこでは彼とトレウーホフのあいだで口論が燃え上がった。

sentences.ru: Покуда строились и монтировались трамвайная станция и депо, старгородцы только отпускали шуточки.
sentences.en: While the tram power station and depot were being built and fitted out, the people of Stargorod did nothing but crack jokes.
sentences.zh: 在电车发电站和车库建造安装期间，斯塔尔戈罗德人只是不断地开着玩笑。
sentences.ja: 路面電車の発電所と車庫が建設され据え付けられているあいだ、スタルゴロドの市民たちはただ冗談を飛ばすばかりだった。

sentences.ru: В «Старгородской правде» трамвайным вопросом занялся известный всему городу фельетонист Принц Датский, писавший теперь под псевдонимом «Маховик».
sentences.en: In the Stargorod Pravda the tram question was taken up by the feuilletonist known to the whole town as the Prince of Denmark, who now wrote under the pen-name 'Flywheel'.
sentences.zh: 在《斯塔尔戈罗德真理报》上，全城闻名的小品文作家“丹麦王子”接手了电车问题，如今他改用笔名“飞轮”。
sentences.ja: 『スタルゴロド・プラウダ』では、町中に知られた風刺コラムニスト「デンマークの王子」――いまは「はずみ車」という筆名で書いていた――が路面電車問題を取り上げた。

sentences.ru: Не меньше трех раз в неделю Маховик разражался большим бытовым очерком о ходе постройки.
sentences.en: No fewer than three times a week Flywheel burst forth with a long human-interest sketch on the progress of the construction.
sentences.zh: 每周至少三次，“飞轮”都要抛出一篇长长的生活特写，报道工程进展。
sentences.ja: 週に三度は下らぬ頻度で、はずみ車は工事の進捗をめぐる長い生活ルポをぶちまけた。

sentences.ru: Третья полоса газеты, изобиловавшая заметками под скептическими заголовками: «Мало пахнет клубом», «По слабым точкам», «Осмотры нужны, но при чем тут блеск и длинные хвосты», «Хорошо и… плохо», «Чему мы рады и чему нет», «Подкрутить вредителей просвещения» и «С бумажным морем пора покончить» — стала дарить читателей солнечными и бодрыми заголовками очерков Маховика: «Как строим, как живем», «Гигант скоро заработает», «Скромный строитель» и далее, в том же духе.
sentences.en: The paper's third page, which had abounded in items under sceptical headlines — 'Not Much Smell of a Club', 'On the Weak Spots', 'Inspections Are Needed, but What Have Glitter and Long Tails to Do with It', 'Good and… Bad', 'What We're Glad of and What We're Not', 'Tighten the Screws on the Wreckers of Education' and 'Time to Finish with the Sea of Paper' — began to treat its readers to the sunny and cheerful headlines of Flywheel's sketches: 'How We Build, How We Live', 'The Giant Will Soon Start Up', 'A Modest Builder' and so on, in the same vein.
sentences.zh: 报纸的第三版本来充斥着标题满是怀疑口吻的短讯——《俱乐部味儿不浓》《说说薄弱环节》《检查是需要的，可跟排场和长尾巴有什么关系》《好的……和坏的》《我们为什么高兴，为什么不高兴》《给教育界的害群之马上上紧》《该跟文牍的海洋一刀两断了》——如今开始用“飞轮”特写那些阳光明媚、朝气蓬勃的标题款待读者：《我们怎样建设，我们怎样生活》《巨人即将开动》《谦逊的建设者》，诸如此类，不一而足。
sentences.ja: 新聞の第三面は、それまで「クラブの匂いが薄い」「弱点を突く」「点検は必要だが、派手さと長い尻尾は何の関係がある」「良いこと……と悪いこと」「われらの喜ぶこと、喜ばぬこと」「教育界の害虫を締め上げよ」「紙の海とはもう手を切る時だ」といった懐疑的な見出しの記事で溢れていたが、いまや読者に、はずみ車のルポの晴れやかで元気いっぱいの見出しを贈るようになった――「いかに建て、いかに生きるか」「巨人はまもなく動き出す」「つつましき建設者」、以下同様の調子である。

sentences.ru: Треухов с дрожью разворачивал газету и, чувствуя отвращение к братьям писателям, читал о своей особе бодрые строки:
sentences.en: Treukhov would unfold the paper with a shudder and, feeling disgust for the brotherhood of writers, read the cheerful lines about his own person:
sentences.zh: 特列乌霍夫哆嗦着打开报纸，怀着对作家同行们的厌恶，读着那些关于他本人的朝气蓬勃的字句：
sentences.ja: トレウーホフは震えながら新聞を広げ、物書きの同業者たちへの嫌悪を覚えつつ、自分の身の上について書かれた元気いっぱいの文章を読むのだった。

sentences.ru: «…Подымаюсь по стропилам.
sentences.en: "…I climb up the rafters.
sentences.zh: “……我沿着桁架往上爬。
sentences.ja: 「……私は小屋組を登ってゆく。

sentences.ru: Ветер шумит в уши.
sentences.en: The wind roars in my ears.
sentences.zh: 风在耳边呼啸。
sentences.ja: 風が耳もとで鳴る。

sentences.ru: Наверху — он, этот невзрачный строитель нашей мощной трамвайной станции, этот худенький с виду, курносый человек, в затрапезной фуражке с молоточками.
sentences.en: Up top is he — this unprepossessing builder of our mighty tram power station, this slight-looking, snub-nosed man in a shabby engineer's cap with the crossed-hammers badge.
sentences.zh: 上面就是他——我们那强大的电车发电站的这位其貌不扬的建设者，这个看上去瘦小、翘鼻子的人，戴着一顶带交叉小锤徽章的旧工程师制帽。
sentences.ja: 上にいるのが彼だ――われらが強大なる路面電車発電所の、この風采の上がらぬ建設者、この見るからに痩せた、鼻の上を向いた男、交差した小槌の徽章のついたよれよれの技師帽をかぶった男が。

sentences.ru: Вспоминаю: «На берегу пустынных волн стоял он, дум великих полн».
sentences.en: I recall: 'On the shore of desolate waves he stood, full of lofty thoughts' (Pushkin, The Bronze Horseman).
sentences.zh: 我想起了：“他伫立在荒凉的波涛岸边，满怀宏伟的思想”（普希金《青铜骑士》）。
sentences.ja: 私は思い出す――「荒涼たる波の岸辺に彼は立ち、大いなる思いに満ちて」（プーシキン『青銅の騎士』）。

sentences.ru: Подхожу.
sentences.en: I go up to him.
sentences.zh: 我走上前去。
sentences.ja: 私は歩み寄る。

sentences.ru: Ни единого ветерка.
sentences.en: Not a breath of wind.
sentences.zh: 没有一丝风。
sentences.ja: 風はそよとも吹かない。

sentences.ru: Стропила не шелохнутся.
sentences.en: The rafters do not stir.
sentences.zh: 桁架纹丝不动。
sentences.ja: 小屋組はびくとも動かない。

sentences.ru: Спрашиваю:
sentences.en: I ask:
sentences.zh: 我问道：
sentences.ja: 私は尋ねる。

sentences.ru: — Как выполняются задания?
sentences.en: 'How are the targets being met?'
sentences.zh: ‘任务完成得怎么样？’
sentences.ja: 『課題はどのように遂行されていますか？』

sentences.ru: Некрасивое лицо строителя,
sentences.en: The builder's plain face,
sentences.zh: 建设者那不好看的脸，
sentences.ja: 建設者の不器量な顔が、

translator_notes: 'Трамвайная станция' here is not a tram stop but the tram system's electric power station, which Treukhov is building along with the depot; it is rendered 'tram power station' / 电车发电站 / 路面電車の発電所 throughout.

The string of headlines on the newspaper's third page ('Not Much Smell of a Club', 'Tighten the Screws on the Wreckers of Education', etc.) parodies the stock phrasing of 1920s Soviet provincial newspapers; the point is their tone, not any real events, and no real articles are referred to.

Gavrilin's sudden shift from the polite 'you' (за вами остановка) to the familiar 'you' (начинай, тебе) when giving Treukhov the go-ahead is deliberate: an official's warm, bluff familiarity, kept in the Japanese and Chinese by switching from polite to plain forms.
